important_parameters.meaning: Specifies the data to insert as rows.

important_features_or_tools.name: MANAGE Permission
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Permission level required to create and modify masking policies on a catalog or schema.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Ensure you have MANAGE permission on the target catalog or schema before attempting to create governed tags or masking policies.

important_features_or_tools.name: EXECUTE Permission
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Permission required to run user-defined functions (UDFs) used in masking policies.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: If your masking policies use UDFs, grant EXECUTE permission to users who need to query masked columns.

practical_workflow.action: Create account groups in Workspace Settings > Identity and access > Groups. Create at least: hr_team, finance_team, marketing_team, us_team, eu_team. Add yourself to hr_team and us_team.
practical_workflow.reason: Groups are the foundation of access control. You need them defined before you can write policies that reference them.

practical_workflow.action: Go to Catalog Explorer > Govern > Governed Tags and create two governed tags: 'domain' with values (hr, finance, marketing) and 'sensitivity' with values (internal, confidential).
practical_workflow.reason: Governed tags are the metadata you will attach to columns. They must be defined before you can use them in masking policies.

practical_workflow.action: Run the CREATE CATALOG and CREATE SCHEMA commands to set up your workspace structure (e.g., abac_tutorial catalog, domain_demo schema).
practical_workflow.reason: Organizing your tables in a dedicated catalog and schema keeps your project clean and makes it easier to apply policies consistently.

practical_workflow.action: Run the CREATE TABLE command to create the employee_records table with columns: id, employee_name, ssn, email, customer_list, cost_center, salary_band, emp_region, department.
practical_workflow.reason: This is the shared table that will be accessed by multiple teams with different permissions. It serves as the target for your masking and filtering policies.

practical_workflow.action: Run the INSERT INTO command to populate the employee_records table with sample data.
practical_workflow.reason: Sample data lets you test your policies before applying them to production data. You can verify that masking and filtering work as expected.

practical_workflow.action: Tag each sensitive column with the 'domain' and 'sensitivity' governed tags. For example, tag 'ssn' with domain='hr' and sensitivity='confidential'.
practical_workflow.reason: Tagging columns is how you tell Databricks which policies to apply. Without tags, the system does not know which columns need protection.

practical_workflow.action: Create masking policies using MATCH COLUMNS with AND conditions to target columns by both domain and sensitivity. Use EXCEPT clauses to exempt each domain's owning group from masking.
practical_workflow.reason: Masking policies enforce the actual access control. AND conditions ensure policies apply only to the right combination of domain and sensitivity. EXCEPT clauses ensure authorized users see unmasked data.

practical_workflow.action: Test the policies by querying the table as different users (or simulating different group memberships). Verify that users see unmasked data for their domain and masked data for other domains.
practical_workflow.reason: Testing confirms that your policies work as intended before deploying to production. It catches configuration errors early.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that a column can belong to multiple domains. The tutorial states 'each column is assigned to exactly one owning group.'
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Each column has a single domain owner. If a column is relevant to multiple teams, decide which team owns it and use row filtering or separate columns for team-specific data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to use EXCEPT clauses, so the owning team also sees masked data.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always include an EXCEPT clause that exempts the owning group from the masking policy. Without it, even authorized users see masked data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using tag names or values that contain sensitive information (e.g., 'salary_data' or 'pii').
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The tutorial warns: 'Do not use tag names, values, or descriptors that could compromise the security of your resources.' Use neutral names like 'domain' and 'sensitivity' instead.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not creating the required groups before writing policies.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Groups must exist before you reference them in policies. Create all groups in Workspace Settings > Identity and access > Groups first.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing 'Internal' and 'Confidential' sensitivity levels. Internal shows partial data (first character + ***), while Confidential shows only ***REDACTED***.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Internal is less aggressive masking (useful for non-critical data), Confidential is full redaction (for highly sensitive data like SSN or salary).

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that users in multiple domain groups see masked data for all domains.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Users in multiple domain groups see all of their domains' columns unmasked. If a user is in both hr_team and finance_team, they see both HR and Finance columns unmasked.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, start by identifying which teams own which columns and what sensitivity level each column needs. Document this in a table (like the one in the tutorial) before tagging.
Use the 'domain' tag to represent team ownership. The tutorial notes the name is arbitrary; you can use 'team', 'department', or 'business_unit' if that fits your organization better.
Combine column masking with row filtering (e.g., emp_region) for layered security. Users see only rows relevant to their region and columns relevant to their team.
Test policies with sample data before applying to production. Use the INSERT INTO sample data provided in the tutorial to verify masking and filtering behavior.
Ensure you have MANAGE permission on the catalog or schema where you create policies, and that users have EXECUTE permission on any UDFs used in masking.
Remember that governed tags are stored as plain text and may be replicated globally. Do not use them to store actual sensitive data; use them only as metadata to control access.

When adding users to groups, remember that group membership determines what data they see. A user in hr_team sees HR columns unmasked; a user not in hr_team sees them masked according to the sensitivity level.

source_content:
Tag each sensitive column with both its `domain` and `sensitivity` values. These two tags together allow each policy to target a specific domain and sensitivity combination using AND conditions in `MATCH COLUMNS`. The `emp_region` column gets a key-only `region` tag because the policy only needs to identify the column rather than check a specific value.

```
-- HR domain
ALTER TABLE employee_records
  ALTER COLUMN employee_name SET TAGS ('domain' = 'hr', 'sensitivity' = 'internal');
ALTER TABLE employee_records
  ALTER COLUMN ssn SET TAGS ('domain' = 'hr', 'sensitivity' = 'confidential');
-- Marketing domain
ALTER TABLE employee_records
  ALTER COLUMN email SET TAGS ('domain' = 'marketing', 'sensitivity' = 'internal');
ALTER TABLE employee_records
  ALTER COLUMN customer_list SET TAGS ('domain' = 'marketing', 'sensitivity' = 'confidential');
-- Finance domain
ALTER TABLE employee_records
  ALTER COLUMN cost_center SET TAGS ('domain' = 'finance', 'sensitivity' = 'internal');
ALTER TABLE employee_records
  ALTER COLUMN salary_band SET TAGS ('domain' = 'finance', 'sensitivity' = 'confidential');
-- Region tag for row filtering
ALTER TABLE employee_records
  ALTER COLUMN emp_region SET TAGS ('region' = '');
```

The row filter UDF accepts the row's region value and an allowed region as a static argument, and returns `TRUE` when they match. Passing the allowed region as a constant keeps the UDF simple and reusable. Each row filter policy targets one group and passes the region that group is authorized to see.

```
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION abac_tutorial.domain_demo.region_filter(region_val STRING, allowed_region STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN region_val = allowed_region;
```
Create a partial mask UDF for internal columns and a full redact UDF for confidential columns.

```
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION abac_tutorial.domain_demo.partial_mask(val STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CONCAT(LEFT(val, 1), '***');
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION abac_tutorial.domain_demo.redact(val STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN '***REDACTED***';
```

Create one row filter policy per region. Each policy targets a specific group and passes the allowed region as a constant via `USING COLUMNS`.

```
CREATE POLICY region_filter_us
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
ROW FILTER abac_tutorial.domain_demo.region_filter
TO `us_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('region') AS region_col
USING COLUMNS (region_col, 'us');
CREATE POLICY region_filter_eu
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
ROW FILTER abac_tutorial.domain_demo.region_filter
TO `eu_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('region') AS region_col
USING COLUMNS (region_col, 'eu');
```
An alternative is to embed the group logic inside the UDF using identity functions such as `is_account_group_member()`. That approach uses a single policy with no static values, but moves the group-to-region mapping into the UDF. Use whichever fits your organization.

Create one policy per domain and sensitivity combination. Each policy uses AND to match columns with a specific `domain` AND `sensitivity` level, and `EXCEPT` to exempt the owning domain group.

Because each column has exactly one `domain` value and one `sensitivity` value, each column is matched by exactly one policy per user. There are no conflicts.

reference_note.title: Column Tagging and Access Control Policies in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Use column tags with `domain` and `sensitivity` values to control who can see sensitive data in Databricks tables. Create UDFs (User Defined Functions) to mask, redact, or filter data based on these tags. Build policies that match specific tag combinations and apply different rules to different user groups.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Labels you attach to table columns that describe what kind of data they contain. Each tag has a key (like 'domain' or 'sensitivity') and a value (like 'hr' or 'confidential'). A single column can have multiple tags.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tags let you group columns by their sensitivity level and business domain, so you can write one policy that applies to many columns at once instead of managing each column individually.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Two specific tags used together: `domain` identifies which business area owns the data (hr, marketing, finance), and `sensitivity` describes how protected it needs to be (internal, confidential). Together they create a unique combination for each column.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Using both tags together lets you create precise policies. For example, you can write a rule that says 'mask all marketing columns with internal sensitivity' without affecting HR internal columns.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A tag with just a key name and no value (like `'region' = ''`). Used when you only need to identify that a column exists, not check what value it contains.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Useful for row filtering where you need to reference a column but don't need to match specific values. Keeps policies simpler and more reusable.

key_concepts.concept: User Defined Functions (UDFs) for Data Protection
key_concepts.simple_explanation: Custom functions you write that decide what data a user can see. They can mask (hide part of) data, redact (hide all of) data, or filter rows based on conditions.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: UDFs let you apply consistent data protection rules across your entire Databricks workspace without manually managing access to each column.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Rules that decide which rows a user can see based on a condition (like their region). The policy calls a UDF that returns TRUE or FALSE for each row.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Lets you restrict data at the row level, so users in the US team only see US data, EU team only sees EU data, etc.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Rules that hide or partially hide column values for certain users. Masking shows some characters (like 'J***' for a name), redaction hides everything ('***REDACTED***').
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Lets you show sensitive columns to some users while protecting the data from others, without creating separate tables or views.

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Attaches one or more tags to a specific column in a table. You specify the tag key and value as key-value pairs.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you first set up your tables and need to label columns with their domain and sensitivity level

important_parameters.meaning: The business area that owns this column (e.g., 'hr', 'marketing', 'finance')
How sensitive the data is (e.g., 'internal', 'confidential')

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a new UDF or replaces an existing one. The function contains logic that will be executed by policies to protect data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to define how data should be masked, redacted, or filtered

important_parameters.meaning: The data type the function returns (BOOLEAN for filters, STRING for masking/redaction)

important_features_or_tools.name: Partial Mask UDF
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A UDF that hides most of a value but shows the first character. Example: 'John' becomes 'J***'
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: For internal sensitivity columns where users need to identify the data but don't need the full value

important_parameters.meaning: The column value to be masked

important_features_or_tools.name: Redact UDF
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A UDF that completely hides a value by replacing it with '***REDACTED***'
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: For confidential sensitivity columns where users should not see any part of the actual value

important_parameters.meaning: The column value to be redacted

important_features_or_tools.name: Region Filter UDF
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A UDF that compares a row's region value with an allowed region and returns TRUE if they match, FALSE otherwise. Used for row filtering.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to restrict which rows users can see based on their region or location

important_parameters.meaning: The region value from the current row
The region that the current user is authorized to see (passed as a constant by the policy)

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE POLICY
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a data access policy that applies a UDF to specific columns or rows for specific user groups
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to enforce data protection rules across your tables

important_parameters.meaning: Specifies which UDF to use for filtering rows
The user group or principal this policy applies to
Specifies which columns the policy applies to using tag matching
Specifies which columns are passed as arguments to the UDF, and what static values to pass

important_features_or_tools.name: MATCH COLUMNS with has_tag()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A way to select which columns a policy applies to by checking if they have specific tags. You can use AND to match multiple tags on the same column.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want a policy to apply to all columns with a certain tag combination, rather than listing columns individually

important_parameters.meaning: Matches columns that have both a domain tag AND a sensitivity tag

important_features_or_tools.name: EXCEPT clause in policies
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Exempts a specific user group from a policy. Used to prevent a group from being restricted by a policy they shouldn't be subject to.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to protect data from most users but allow the owning domain group to see it unmasked

important_features_or_tools.name: is_account_group_member() function
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks identity function that checks if the current user is a member of a specific group. Can be used inside UDFs to embed group logic.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: As an alternative to passing static values in policies; lets you write one policy instead of multiple policies per group

practical_workflow.action: Identify all sensitive columns in your table and decide their domain (hr, marketing, finance, etc.) and sensitivity level (internal, confidential)
practical_workflow.reason: You need to know what to tag before you can create policies

practical_workflow.action: Use ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS to tag each sensitive column with both 'domain' and 'sensitivity' tags
practical_workflow.reason: Tags are the foundation that policies use to identify which columns to protect

practical_workflow.action: Create UDFs for masking (partial_mask), redacting (redact), and filtering (region_filter) based on your protection needs
practical_workflow.reason: UDFs define the actual protection logic that will be applied to your data

practical_workflow.action: Create row filter policies (one per region or group) that use MATCH COLUMNS to find columns with the 'region' tag and call your region_filter UDF
practical_workflow.reason: Row filters restrict which rows each user group can see

practical_workflow.action: Create masking policies (one per domain + sensitivity combination) that use MATCH COLUMNS with AND conditions to find columns with specific domain AND sensitivity combinations, and call your partial_mask UDF
practical_workflow.reason: Masking policies hide sensitive data while still allowing users to see that data exists

practical_workflow.action: Create redaction policies (one per domain + sensitivity combination) for confidential columns, using EXCEPT to exempt the owning domain group
practical_workflow.reason: Redaction completely hides confidential data from unauthorized users while letting the owning team see it

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using only one tag (like just 'sensitivity') instead of both 'domain' and 'sensitivity'
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always use both tags together. This lets you create precise policies that target specific domain + sensitivity combinations. A single tag is not specific enough.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Creating one policy per column instead of using tag matching
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use MATCH COLUMNS with has_tag() to write one policy that applies to many columns at once. This is much simpler to maintain.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to use EXCEPT to exempt the owning domain group from redaction policies
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The domain that owns sensitive data should always be able to see it unredacted. Use EXCEPT to prevent the policy from applying to that group.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Passing the allowed region as a variable instead of a constant in row filter policies
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Pass the allowed region as a static constant (like 'us' or 'eu') in USING COLUMNS. This keeps the UDF simple and reusable. Create one policy per region instead.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that each column will be matched by multiple policies
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Because each column has exactly one domain value and one sensitivity value, each column is matched by exactly one policy per user. There are no conflicts.

project_usage_notes: Start by tagging your most sensitive columns (like salary, SSN, customer lists) with both domain and sensitivity tags. You can add more columns later.
Create your UDFs once and reuse them across multiple policies. For example, the same partial_mask UDF can be used in policies for HR internal, Marketing internal, and Finance internal columns.
Use one row filter policy per region or location. Each policy passes a different allowed_region constant to the same region_filter UDF.
Use one masking policy per domain + sensitivity combination (e.g., one for 'hr' + 'internal', one for 'marketing' + 'internal', etc.). This ensures each column is protected by exactly one policy.
Test your policies with different user groups to make sure masking and redaction work as expected, and that row filters show the correct rows.

If your organization has many groups and regions, consider using is_account_group_member() inside your UDFs instead of creating multiple policies with static values. This reduces the number of policies you need to maintain.

source_content:
Apply a partial mask to internal-level columns for users outside the owning domain.

```
CREATE POLICY mask_internal_hr
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
COLUMN MASK abac_tutorial.domain_demo.partial_mask
TO `account users` EXCEPT `hr_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS (
  has_tag_value('domain', 'hr')
  AND has_tag_value('sensitivity', 'internal')
) AS m
ON COLUMN m;
CREATE POLICY mask_internal_finance
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
COLUMN MASK abac_tutorial.domain_demo.partial_mask
TO `account users` EXCEPT `finance_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS (
  has_tag_value('domain', 'finance')
  AND has_tag_value('sensitivity', 'internal')
) AS m
ON COLUMN m;
CREATE POLICY mask_internal_marketing
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
COLUMN MASK abac_tutorial.domain_demo.partial_mask
TO `account users` EXCEPT `marketing_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS (
  has_tag_value('domain', 'marketing')
  AND has_tag_value('sensitivity', 'internal')
) AS m
ON COLUMN m;
```

Fully redact confidential-level columns for users outside the owning domain.

```
CREATE POLICY mask_confidential_hr
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
COLUMN MASK abac_tutorial.domain_demo.redact
TO `account users` EXCEPT `hr_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS (
  has_tag_value('domain', 'hr')
  AND has_tag_value('sensitivity', 'confidential')
) AS m
ON COLUMN m;
CREATE POLICY mask_confidential_finance
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
COLUMN MASK abac_tutorial.domain_demo.redact
TO `account users` EXCEPT `finance_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS (
  has_tag_value('domain', 'finance')
  AND has_tag_value('sensitivity', 'confidential')
) AS m
ON COLUMN m;
CREATE POLICY mask_confidential_marketing
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.domain_demo
COLUMN MASK abac_tutorial.domain_demo.redact
TO `account users` EXCEPT `marketing_team`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS (
  has_tag_value('domain', 'marketing')
  AND has_tag_value('sensitivity', 'confidential')
) AS m
ON COLUMN m;
```

All seven policies (two row filters and six column masks) are now active. Run the following query and verify that the results match what your group membership permits.

```
SELECT * FROM abac_tutorial.domain_demo.employee_records;
```

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Alice Johnson | 123-45-6789 |
 | ***REDACTED*** |

| 5 | Eva Martinez | 567-89-0123 |

HR columns (`employee_name`, `ssn`) are unmasked. Marketing internal (`email`) is partially masked and confidential (`customer_list`) is redacted. Finance internal (`cost_center`) is partially masked and confidential (`salary_band`) is redacted.

**Finance team member in EU region** (`finance_team` + `eu_team`):

| id | employee_name | ssn | customer_list | cost_center | salary_band | emp_region | department | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 |

| 4 |

Finance columns (`cost_center`, `salary_band`) are unmasked. All other domain columns are masked or redacted.

**User in  hr_team + marketing_team + us_team:**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

reference_note.title: Column-Level Masking Policies with Domain-Based Access Control
reference_note.summary: Databricks allows you to create column masking policies that automatically hide or partially mask sensitive data based on user group membership and column tags. You define policies using CREATE POLICY with COLUMN MASK, specify which columns to mask using tag matching, and control who sees what data by using group membership (EXCEPT clause). When users query tables, the policies automatically apply based on their group membership.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that automatically hides or transforms sensitive column values for certain users. Instead of manually filtering data, you define once who can see what, and Databricks enforces it automatically on every query.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In real projects, you need to protect sensitive data (like salaries, SSNs, customer lists) while still allowing authorized teams to see it. Masking policies ensure consistent, automatic protection without requiring custom code in every query.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: You tag columns with metadata (like domain='hr' and sensitivity='internal'), then write policies that match those tags. Users see different data based on their group membership and the tags on columns.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tags let you scale security policies. Instead of writing a policy for every column, you write one policy that applies to all columns with matching tags. When you add new columns with the same tags, the policy automatically applies.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: You define policies that apply to specific user groups (like hr_team, finance_team). Users in that group see unmasked data; users outside see masked data.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In multi-team projects, different teams need different views of the same data. Group-based policies let each team see only what they need without creating separate tables or databases.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Partial masking shows some information (like the first few characters); full redaction replaces the entire value with ***REDACTED***. You choose which masking function to apply based on sensitivity level.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Some data needs to be completely hidden (confidential salary info), while other data can be partially visible (email addresses). Different sensitivity levels require different masking strategies.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE POLICY
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a new masking policy that automatically applies to columns matching specified conditions
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to define a new rule for masking sensitive data

important_features_or_tools.name: COLUMN MASK
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies that this policy masks column values (as opposed to filtering rows)
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to hide or transform column data rather than hide entire rows

important_features_or_tools.name: ON SCHEMA
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which schema the policy applies to
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When defining the scope of the policy

important_parameters.meaning: The full path to the schema (e.g., abac_tutorial.domain_demo)

important_features_or_tools.name: Masking Function Reference
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Points to a function that transforms the column value (e.g., partial_mask for partial masking, redact for full redaction)
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When specifying how to mask the data

important_parameters.meaning: A masking function that shows partial information (exact behavior depends on function definition)
A masking function that completely hides the value, replacing it with ***REDACTED***

important_features_or_tools.name: TO ... EXCEPT
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which groups the policy applies to. TO `account users` EXCEPT `group_name` means: apply masking to all users except those in group_name
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to mask data for most users but allow specific groups to see unmasked data

important_parameters.meaning: All users in the Databricks account
The group(s) that should NOT have masking applied (they see unmasked data)

important_features_or_tools.name: FOR TABLES MATCH COLUMNS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which columns the policy applies to by matching tag conditions
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to apply a policy to all columns with specific tags

important_features_or_tools.name: has_tag_value()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Checks if a column has a specific tag with a specific value. Used in MATCH COLUMNS to select which columns the policy applies to
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When defining which columns should be masked based on their tags

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the tag to check (e.g., 'domain', 'sensitivity')
The value the tag should have (e.g., 'hr', 'internal', 'confidential')

important_features_or_tools.name: AND operator in MATCH COLUMNS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Combines multiple tag conditions. Both conditions must be true for the policy to apply
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to mask only columns that match multiple criteria (e.g., domain='hr' AND sensitivity='internal')

important_features_or_tools.name: AS m ON COLUMN m
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Aliases the matched columns as 'm' and applies the masking function to those columns
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: This is required syntax when using MATCH COLUMNS

practical_workflow.action: Tag your columns with metadata (domain and sensitivity). For example, tag the 'ssn' column with domain='hr' and sensitivity='confidential'
practical_workflow.reason: Tags are the foundation of ABAC. Policies match columns by tags, so you need to tag columns before creating policies

practical_workflow.action: Define masking functions (like partial_mask and redact) that transform column values. These functions determine how data is hidden
practical_workflow.reason: Masking policies reference these functions. You need them defined before creating policies

practical_workflow.action: Create a COLUMN MASK policy for each combination of domain and sensitivity level. For example, create one policy for HR internal columns, another for HR confidential columns, etc.
practical_workflow.reason: Different sensitivity levels need different masking strategies. Internal data gets partial masking; confidential data gets full redaction

practical_workflow.action: In each policy, use TO `account users` EXCEPT `group_name` to specify which group can see unmasked data
practical_workflow.reason: This ensures only authorized teams see sensitive data. All other users see masked data

practical_workflow.action: Use MATCH COLUMNS with has_tag_value() to specify which columns the policy applies to. Combine conditions with AND for multiple tag requirements
practical_workflow.reason: This makes policies reusable. One policy applies to all columns with matching tags, not just specific columns

practical_workflow.action: Query the table normally (SELECT * FROM table). Databricks automatically applies all active policies based on your group membership
practical_workflow.reason: Masking is transparent to users. You don't need to write special queries; policies enforce automatically

practical_workflow.action: Verify results by checking what data is visible/masked for different user groups
practical_workflow.reason: Ensures policies are working as intended and users see only what they should

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking you need to create a separate policy for every column
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use tags and MATCH COLUMNS to create one policy that applies to many columns. For example, one policy for all 'internal' sensitivity columns in the 'hr' domain

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing TO `account users` EXCEPT `group` with TO `group`
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: TO `account users` EXCEPT `group` means: mask for everyone EXCEPT the group (the group sees unmasked data). If you want the opposite, you'd need a different policy structure

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking partial_mask and redact are built-in functions
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: They are custom masking functions that must be defined in your schema. The content shows them being referenced, but they are user-defined functions

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming policies apply only to specific queries
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Policies apply automatically to all queries on the table. Every SELECT query respects the policies based on the user's group membership

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not understanding that users in multiple groups see unmasked data for all their groups' domains
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If a user is in both hr_team and marketing_team, they see unmasked HR columns AND unmasked marketing columns. Masking only applies to domains they don't belong to

project_usage_notes: In a real multi-team project, use column masking to let teams share the same table without seeing each other's sensitive data. For example, HR, Finance, and Marketing can all query employee_records, but each team sees only their own domain's unmasked data
Tag columns consistently (domain and sensitivity) so policies scale automatically. When you add new columns with the same tags, existing policies apply without modification
Use partial masking for data that needs some visibility (like email addresses where you show the domain but hide the username) and full redaction for highly sensitive data (like SSNs or salaries)
Test policies with different user groups to verify they work correctly. The example shows how different groups see different results from the same query
Combine column masking with row-level policies (not shown in this content) for comprehensive data protection. Column masking hides sensitive columns; row filters hide sensitive rows
Document which tags and masking functions you use so team members understand the security model and can tag new columns correctly

reference_note.title: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) with Policies and Tags in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Databricks uses policies and tags to control who sees what data. Each column gets tagged with a domain (like 'hr' or 'marketing') and sensitivity level (like 'internal' or 'confidential'). Policies then automatically mask or filter data based on the user's group membership. The EXCEPT clause is key: policies apply to everyone except the group that owns the data, so owners see raw data while others see masked data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A policy is a rule that says 'apply this masking/filtering to all account users EXCEPT those in this specific group.' If you're in the owning group, you're excluded and see raw data. If you're not, the policy applies and data is masked.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This is how Databricks prevents data leaks while letting data owners see everything. In a real project, you need to understand that being in the right group determines what you see.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Each column is tagged with two things: a domain (like 'hr', 'marketing', 'finance') and a sensitivity level (like 'internal' or 'confidential'). These tags tell policies which columns to protect.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tags are how you organize which data belongs to which team and how sensitive it is. This makes policies reusable and scalable.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: If a user is in multiple groups (for example, both 'hr_team' and 'marketing_team'), they are excluded from policies for both domains. They see raw data for both HR and Marketing columns.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In real projects, people often work across teams. Multi-group membership means one user can have the right access to multiple datasets without creating conflicting policies.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When you add a new domain (like 'Legal'), you only add new groups, tags, and policies for that domain. Existing policies don't change.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Your access control system grows without breaking existing rules. This is critical for projects that expand over time.

important_features_or_tools.name: Policy
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A policy is a rule that masks or filters data based on user group membership. It uses the EXCEPT clause to exclude the owning group from the masking rule.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use policies whenever you need to automatically hide or redact sensitive data from users who shouldn't see it.

important_parameters.meaning: Specifies which group is excluded from the policy. Members of this group see raw data; everyone else sees masked data.
important_parameters.example_value: EXCEPT account_users IN (SELECT principal_id FROM account_groups WHERE display_name = 'hr_team')

important_features_or_tools.name: Governed tags (domain, sensitivity, region)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Tags are metadata labels applied to columns. They categorize data by domain (hr, marketing, finance, legal), sensitivity (internal, confidential), and region (us, eu). Policies use these tags to decide what to protect.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Tag every column in your tables so policies know which data to protect and how.

important_parameters.meaning: Identifies which team or department owns the column (hr, marketing, finance, legal, etc.)
Identifies how sensitive the data is (internal, confidential, etc.)
Identifies geographic region restrictions (us, eu, etc.)

important_features_or_tools.name: Account groups (hr_team, finance_team, marketing_team, us_team, eu_team)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Groups are sets of users. Policies use group membership to decide who is excluded from masking. Users in the owning group see raw data; users not in the group see masked data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Create a group for each domain or region. Add users to groups based on their role or team.

important_features_or_tools.name: Masking functions (partial_mask, redact)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Functions that transform data to hide sensitive information. partial_mask shows only part of the value; redact hides it completely.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use in policies to transform sensitive columns before non-owners see them.

important_features_or_tools.name: Filtering functions (region_filter)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Functions that filter rows based on user attributes or group membership. For example, region_filter might show only rows matching the user's region.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use in policies to restrict which rows users can see based on their location or team.

important_features_or_tools.name: DROP POLICY command
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Removes a policy from a schema. Syntax: DROP POLICY policy_name ON SCHEMA schema_name.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to delete a policy (for example, when cleaning up a tutorial or removing outdated access rules).

important_parameters.meaning: The exact name of the policy to drop
The schema where the policy is defined

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer UI
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks UI tool for managing governed tags. Use it to create, edit, and remove tags.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to manage tags visually instead of using SQL commands.

important_features_or_tools.name: Workspace settings
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks UI section where you manage account groups and user memberships.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to create groups or add/remove users from groups.

practical_workflow.action: Create account groups for each domain and region (hr_team, marketing_team, finance_team, us_team, eu_team) in workspace settings.
practical_workflow.reason: Policies use group membership to decide who sees raw data. You need groups before you can create policies.

practical_workflow.action: Create governed tags for domain, sensitivity, and region in Catalog Explorer. Add allowed values (hr, marketing, finance, legal for domain; internal, confidential for sensitivity; us, eu for region).
practical_workflow.reason: Tags are the metadata that policies read to decide what to protect. You must define tags before tagging columns.

practical_workflow.action: Tag all columns in your tables with domain, sensitivity, and region values.
practical_workflow.reason: Policies only protect tagged columns. Untagged columns are not protected.

practical_workflow.action: Create masking and filtering functions (partial_mask, redact, region_filter) in your schema.
practical_workflow.reason: Policies call these functions to transform data. You need the functions before you can use them in policies.

practical_workflow.action: Create policies that use EXCEPT to exclude the owning group. For example: 'Apply partial_mask to all account users EXCEPT those in hr_team for columns tagged domain=hr and sensitivity=internal.'
practical_workflow.reason: Policies are the rules that actually protect data. The EXCEPT clause ensures owners see raw data while others see masked data.

practical_workflow.action: Test by logging in as different users (in different groups) and querying the same table. Verify that owners see raw data and non-owners see masked data.
practical_workflow.reason: Testing confirms your policies work as intended before deploying to production.

practical_workflow.action: To add a new domain (like Legal), create a new group (legal_team), add the domain value to the domain tag, create new policies for that domain, and tag the new columns.
practical_workflow.reason: This workflow ensures new domains are protected without breaking existing policies.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking a policy applies to the owning group. Actually, the EXCEPT clause excludes the owning group, so policies do NOT apply to them.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Remember: EXCEPT means 'everyone except this group.' The owning group is excluded and sees raw data. Everyone else sees masked data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to tag columns. If a column is not tagged, policies won't protect it.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Tag every column with domain and sensitivity. Untagged columns are not protected by any policy.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Creating separate policies for each user instead of using groups. This doesn't scale.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always use groups. Policies apply to groups, not individual users. One user can be in multiple groups.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking you need to change existing policies when adding a new domain. You don't.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Adding a new domain only requires new groups, new tag values, and new policies. Existing policies stay the same.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not understanding that multi-group users are excluded from multiple policies. A user in both hr_team and marketing_team sees raw data for both HR and Marketing columns.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Multi-group membership is a feature, not a bug. It naturally gives users access to multiple domains without policy conflicts.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, start by identifying your domains (HR, Marketing, Finance, Legal, etc.) and creating a group for each. This is your foundation.
Tag every column in every table with domain and sensitivity. This is tedious but essential. Without tags, policies can't protect data.
Use the EXCEPT clause pattern for all policies: 'Apply masking to all account users EXCEPT the owning group.' This is the standard Databricks approach.
Test policies with multiple users in different groups before going to production. Verify that owners see raw data and non-owners see masked data.
When adding a new domain or expanding access, only add new groups, tags, and policies. Never modify existing policies unless you're fixing a bug.
Use Catalog Explorer UI for managing tags and workspace settings for managing groups. These tools make it easier than writing SQL.
Document which columns belong to which domain and sensitivity level. This helps new team members understand the data governance model.
If you need to remove all policies and start over, use the DROP POLICY commands provided. Then use Catalog Explorer to remove tags and workspace settings to remove groups.

source_content:
You can share tables and views protected by ABAC policies through OpenSharing if the share owner is exempted from the policies on the provider side. This page covers how to share tables with row filters and column masks and how to handle views when you need to enforce policies on the recipient side.

- Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above, or serverless compute.
- Account admin or workspace admin permissions (to create governed tags).
- `MANAGE`permission on the target catalog or schema.
- `EXECUTE`on the UDFs.
- OpenSharing configured between the provider and recipient. See What is OpenSharing?.

Share owners can share tables secured by ABAC policies through OpenSharing if they meet both of these conditions:

- They have the required OpenSharing permissions.
- They are exempt from the ABAC policies (listed in the `EXCEPT`clause).

The following example shows a provider-side policy where the share owner is exempted:

```
-- Provider: row filter policy with the share owner exempted
CREATE POLICY hide_eu_customers
ON CATALOG provider_catalog
ROW FILTER hide_eu
TO `account users`
EXCEPT 'share_owner_group'
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('geo_region') AS region
USING COLUMNS (region);
-- Add the table to the share
CREATE SHARE employees_share;
ALTER SHARE employees_share ADD TABLE provider_catalog.hr.employees;
GRANT SELECT ON SHARE employees_share TO RECIPIENT `recipient_org`;
```
The provider's ABAC policy doesn't govern the recipient's access. Because the share owner is exempt from the provider-side policy, the recipient sees unfiltered or unmasked data by default. Recipients can apply their own ABAC policies to shared tables to enforce access control on their side.

- For share providers, see Add tables and schemas secured by ABAC policies to a share.
- For share recipients, see Read ABAC-secured data and apply ABAC policies.

Share owners can also share views that reference ABAC-protected base tables. As with sharing tables directly, the share owner must be exempt from ABAC policies on the underlying tables.

```
-- Provider: row filter policy with the share owner exempted
CREATE POLICY hide_eu_customers
ON CATALOG provider_catalog
ROW FILTER hide_eu
TO `account users`
EXCEPT 'share_owner_group'
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('geo_region') AS region
USING COLUMNS (region);
-- Add the view to the share
ALTER SHARE employees_share ADD VIEW provider_catalog.hr.employees_view AS hr.employees_view;
GRANT SELECT ON SHARE employees_share TO RECIPIENT `recipient_org`;
```
If you were sharing views before April 23, 2026, you might need to update your ABAC policies. Before this date, the **view owner** needed to be exempt from policies on the underlying tables. Starting April 23, 2026, the **share owner** must be exempt instead. If Databricks has contacted you as a potentially impacted customer, you have until July 22, 2026 to update your `EXCEPT` clauses.

Because ABAC policies can only be set on tables, not views, if you need recipient-side users to consume data through views and sensitive data must be protected, share the base tables and set ABAC policies on them. The recipient creates views locally over the shared tables, and the policies on the base tables are respected when data is accessed through those views. You don't need to share provider-side views in this case.

This approach works as follows:

- **Share only the base tables, not the views.**On the recipient side, the shared tables appear in a read-only delta share schema.
- **Apply ABAC policies to the source tables on the provider side and to the shared tables on the recipient side.**The provider's policy controls access on the provider side. The recipient creates a policy to control access for users on the recipient side.
- **Create views at the recipient on top of the shared base tables in a separate schema.**Because OpenSharing schemas are read-only, recipient-local views must be created in a different schema. If you set ABAC policies on the OpenSharing tables, these policies are respected when users access the data through the recipient-local views.

```
-- Recipient: apply an ABAC policy to the shared table
CREATE POLICY hide_eu_customers
ON CATALOG recipient_catalog
ROW FILTER hide_eu
TO `account users`
EXCEPT 'recipient_admins'
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('geo_region') AS region
USING COLUMNS (region);
-- Create a view in a separate schema (delta share schema is read-only)
CREATE VIEW recipient_catalog.analytics.employees_view AS
  SELECT * FROM recipient_catalog.delta_share_schema.employees;
```

reference_note.title: Sharing ABAC-Protected Tables and Views Through OpenSharing
reference_note.summary: OpenSharing allows you to share tables and views protected by Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) policies, but only if the share owner is exempted from those policies on the provider side. Recipients can then apply their own ABAC policies to control access on their side. For views, share the base tables instead and let recipients create their own views locally to ensure policies are enforced correctly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A security system that controls who can see which rows and columns of data based on tags and policies. Row filters hide certain rows; column masks hide certain columns.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When sharing sensitive data through OpenSharing, you need to understand how ABAC policies work on both the provider and recipient sides to ensure data is protected correctly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: The person or group sharing the data must be listed in the EXCEPT clause of the ABAC policy so they can see all the data and share it without restrictions.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Without exemption, the share owner cannot access the full dataset to share it, and recipients will only see filtered/masked data by default.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Provider-side policies control access on the provider's Databricks workspace. Recipient-side policies control access for users in the recipient's workspace. They work independently.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You need to set up policies on both sides if you want to enforce access control at both locations. The provider's policy doesn't automatically apply to the recipient.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When you receive shared tables through OpenSharing, they appear in a read-only schema that you cannot modify directly.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: If you need to create views for recipients, you must create them in a separate schema, not in the read-only OpenSharing schema.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE POLICY
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates an ABAC policy that applies row filters or column masks to tables based on tags and conditions.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to restrict which rows or columns users can see in a table.

important_parameters.meaning: Hides entire rows from users who don't meet the policy condition
Lists groups or users who are exempt from the policy and can see all data
Applies the policy to columns that have a specific tag
Specifies which users or groups the policy applies to

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE SHARE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a new share that you can add tables and views to and grant access to recipients.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to set up a new OpenSharing share to distribute data to another organization.

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER SHARE ... ADD TABLE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Adds a table to an existing share so it can be accessed by the recipient.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to include a specific table in a share.

important_parameters.meaning: The full path to the table being shared (catalog.schema.table)

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER SHARE ... ADD VIEW
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Adds a view to an existing share so it can be accessed by the recipient.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to share a view instead of a base table. Note: best practice is to share base tables and let recipients create views.

important_parameters.meaning: The full path to the view being shared
The name the view will have in the recipient's schema

important_features_or_tools.name: GRANT SELECT ON SHARE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Grants a recipient organization permission to access the shared tables and views.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: After adding tables or views to a share, to give the recipient permission to read them.

important_parameters.meaning: The recipient organization identifier

important_features_or_tools.name: Governed Tags
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Tags that are used in ABAC policies to mark columns or tables with metadata (like 'geo_region'). Only account admins or workspace admins can create them.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to apply ABAC policies based on data characteristics. You must create tags before creating policies that reference them.

practical_workflow.action: Ensure the share owner is exempted from all ABAC policies on the tables you want to share by adding their group to the EXCEPT clause.
practical_workflow.reason: Without exemption, the share owner cannot access the full dataset to share it, and recipients will only see filtered data.

practical_workflow.action: Create or update ABAC policies on the provider side using CREATE POLICY with ROW FILTER or column masks, ensuring the share owner is in the EXCEPT clause.
practical_workflow.reason: This protects data on the provider side while allowing the share owner to share the full dataset.

practical_workflow.action: Create a share using CREATE SHARE and add tables using ALTER SHARE ... ADD TABLE.
practical_workflow.reason: This sets up the share container and includes the tables you want to distribute.

practical_workflow.action: Grant the recipient organization access using GRANT SELECT ON SHARE ... TO RECIPIENT.
practical_workflow.reason: This gives the recipient permission to read the shared tables.

practical_workflow.action: On the recipient side, apply ABAC policies to the shared tables using CREATE POLICY to control access for recipient-side users.
practical_workflow.reason: Provider-side policies don't apply to recipients, so you must set up recipient-side policies to enforce access control.

practical_workflow.action: If recipients need to use views, create views in a separate schema (not the read-only OpenSharing schema) that reference the shared base tables.
practical_workflow.reason: OpenSharing schemas are read-only, and recipient-side ABAC policies on base tables are respected when accessed through views.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that provider-side ABAC policies automatically apply to recipients.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Provider-side policies only control access on the provider side. Recipients must create their own ABAC policies to enforce access control on their side.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to exempt the share owner from ABAC policies.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The share owner must be listed in the EXCEPT clause of all ABAC policies on tables they want to share. Without exemption, they cannot access the full dataset.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to create views directly in the OpenSharing read-only schema.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: OpenSharing schemas are read-only. Create views in a separate schema on the recipient side, and they will respect ABAC policies on the base tables.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Sharing views instead of base tables when ABAC policies are needed.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Share the base tables instead. ABAC policies can only be set on tables, not views. Recipients create views locally, and policies on base tables are respected when accessed through those views.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not updating EXCEPT clauses after April 23, 2026 when sharing views.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Starting April 23, 2026, the share owner (not the view owner) must be exempt from policies on underlying tables. If you shared views before this date, update your EXCEPT clauses by July 22, 2026.

project_usage_notes: Before sharing any ABAC-protected data, verify that your share owner is in the EXCEPT clause of all relevant policies. This is the first step to enable sharing.
When setting up a real project, plan ABAC policies on both provider and recipient sides. Provider policies protect data during sharing; recipient policies protect data for recipient-side users.
If recipients need to query data through views, share only the base tables and let recipients create views locally in a separate schema. This ensures ABAC policies are enforced correctly.
Ensure you have the required permissions: Account admin or workspace admin (to create governed tags), MANAGE permission on the target catalog or schema, and EXECUTE on any UDFs used in policies.
Use Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above, or serverless compute, to ensure ABAC policies and OpenSharing work correctly.
If you shared views before April 23, 2026, check if you need to update your EXCEPT clauses to reflect the new requirement that the share owner (not view owner) must be exempt.
