This page covers requirements, quotas, and limitations for row filter and column mask policies. For GRANT policies (Beta), see ABAC GRANT policies for models (Beta).

This page lists requirements, policy quotas, and current limitations for ABAC row filter and column mask policies in Unity Catalog.

To use ABAC policies, you must use one of the following compute configurations:

- Serverless compute
- Standard compute on Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above
- Dedicated compute on Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above with fine-grained access control filtering enabled

For guidance on running workloads that require older runtimes, see Access from older runtimes.

ABAC policies use governed tags, not ungoverned tags. Governed tags are defined at the account level with access controls that determine who can create, assign, and manage them. For full details, see Governed tags.

After assigning or modifying a tag, it can take a few minutes for the change to take effect.

| Resource | Limit |
|---|---|
| Policies per metastore | 10,000 |
| Policies per catalog or schema | 100 |
| Policies per table | 50 |
| Principals per policy (applies to both  | 20 |
| Column conditions per  | 3 |

For more details, including governed tags quotas, see Service limits.

Standard and dedicated compute on Databricks Runtime versions earlier than 16.4 can't access ABAC-secured tables. If you need certain workloads to continue running on an older runtime, scope the ABAC policy to a specific group instead of applying it broadly. Add only the users or principals you want the policy to apply to that group, and exclude the principal that runs the older-runtime workload using the `EXCEPT` clause. Users outside the group retain full access to the underlying tables. This allows that workload to continue accessing the tables while you transition to a supported runtime.

You can't apply ABAC policies directly to views. However, when a user queries a view that references tables with ABAC policies, those policies are respected when accessing data through the view.

ABAC row filters and column masks on the underlying tables are evaluated using the **session user's identity**, meaning the person running the query. The user sees only the rows and column values they are authorized to access, as defined by the ABAC policies on the base tables. Base table access checks and access checks to dependencies use the view owner's identity, so users can query views without direct privileges on the underlying tables.

The same session user identity model applies when tables with ABAC policies are accessed through functions.

The session user identity model was introduced alongside the ABAC GA release. Previously, policies were evaluated using the view owner's or function definer's identity. For more information, see the April 2026 release notes.

reference_note.title: ABAC Row Filter and Column Mask Policies: Requirements, Quotas, and Limitations
reference_note.summary: ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) policies let you control which rows and columns users can see in tables using governed tags. You need specific compute configurations (Serverless, or Runtime 16.4+), and there are limits on how many policies you can create per resource. Policies are evaluated based on who is running the query, not who owns the view or function.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Rules that control which rows and columns specific users or groups can access in a table. They use governed tags (account-level tags with access controls) to determine access.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This is how you implement fine-grained security in Databricks—ensuring users only see data they're authorized to see, without creating separate tables or views for each user.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Tags defined at the account level with built-in access controls. Only certain people can create, assign, or manage them. ABAC policies must use governed tags, not ungoverned tags.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Governed tags ensure consistent, secure tagging across your organization and prevent unauthorized people from changing tags that control data access.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: ABAC policies are evaluated based on the identity of the person running the query, not the person who created the view or function.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This means users can query views and functions without needing direct permissions on the underlying tables, but they still only see rows and columns they're authorized for.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: ABAC policies only work on Serverless compute, or Standard/Dedicated compute running Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above (with fine-grained access control enabled for Dedicated).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: If your workloads run on older runtimes, they won't be able to access tables protected by ABAC policies. You need to plan your runtime upgrades accordingly.

important_features_or_tools.name: Row Filter Policies
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Controls which rows a user can see in a table based on conditions and governed tags.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want users to see only rows relevant to them (e.g., sales reps see only their region's data).

important_features_or_tools.name: Column Mask Policies
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Controls which columns a user can see or hides sensitive column values based on conditions and governed tags.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to hide sensitive columns (e.g., salary data) from certain users while keeping other columns visible.

important_parameters.meaning: Maximum number of conditions you can define in a single column mask policy

important_features_or_tools.name: EXCEPT clause
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Excludes specific principals (users or groups) from an ABAC policy scope.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to exclude older-runtime workloads from ABAC policies while transitioning to supported runtimes. Scope the policy to a group and use EXCEPT to exclude the principal running the older workload.

important_features_or_tools.name: Serverless Compute
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A compute configuration that fully supports ABAC policies without additional setup.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to use ABAC policies without managing runtime versions or configuration.

important_features_or_tools.name: Standard/Dedicated Compute with Databricks Runtime 16.4+
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Compute configurations that support ABAC policies if running Runtime 16.4 or above (Dedicated requires fine-grained access control filtering enabled).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to use ABAC policies on managed compute clusters.

important_parameters.meaning: Minimum runtime version required for ABAC support
Configuration flag required for Dedicated compute to support ABAC

practical_workflow.action: Verify your compute configuration supports ABAC: use Serverless, or Standard/Dedicated with Runtime 16.4+
practical_workflow.reason: ABAC policies won't work on older runtimes, so you need to confirm your infrastructure is ready before creating policies.

practical_workflow.action: Set up governed tags at the account level with appropriate access controls
practical_workflow.reason: ABAC policies require governed tags to function. You need to define which tags exist and who can manage them.

practical_workflow.action: Assign governed tags to users, groups, or other principals
practical_workflow.reason: Tags are the basis for ABAC policy conditions. Users need tags assigned to match policy rules.

practical_workflow.action: Create row filter or column mask policies on your tables using the governed tags
practical_workflow.reason: Policies define the actual access rules. Row filters control which rows are visible; column masks control which columns are visible.

practical_workflow.action: Wait a few minutes for policy changes to take effect
practical_workflow.reason: Tag assignments and policy modifications have a propagation delay.

practical_workflow.action: Test that users see only the rows and columns they're authorized for
practical_workflow.reason: Verify policies are working as intended before rolling out to production.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using ungoverned tags with ABAC policies
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: ABAC policies only work with governed tags. Governed tags are defined at the account level with access controls. Use those instead.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Expecting ABAC policies to work on Databricks Runtime versions earlier than 16.4
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: ABAC policies require Runtime 16.4 or above (or Serverless). Older runtimes cannot access ABAC-secured tables. Plan a runtime upgrade or use the EXCEPT clause to exclude older workloads temporarily.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Applying ABAC policies directly to views
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You can't apply ABAC policies directly to views. Instead, apply policies to the underlying tables. When users query the view, the table policies are automatically respected.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking the view owner's identity determines what data is visible
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: ABAC policies use the session user's identity (the person running the query), not the view owner's identity. This means users can query views without direct permissions on underlying tables, but they still only see authorized data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Expecting policy changes to take effect immediately
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: After assigning or modifying a tag, wait a few minutes for the change to propagate through the system.

project_usage_notes: When starting a Databricks project with sensitive data, plan your compute infrastructure early: decide whether to use Serverless or upgrade to Runtime 16.4+ before building tables and policies.
Use ABAC policies to implement role-based or attribute-based access without creating separate tables or views for each user group. This reduces maintenance overhead.
If you have legacy workloads running on older runtimes, use the EXCEPT clause to exclude them from ABAC policies while you transition to supported runtimes. This prevents breaking existing jobs.

Remember that ABAC policies are evaluated using the query runner's identity, not the view owner's. This allows you to create shared views that show different data to different users based on their tags.
Respect the quotas: 10,000 policies per metastore, 100 per catalog/schema, 50 per table, 20 principals per policy, and 3 column conditions per policy. Plan your policy structure accordingly.

source_content:
ABAC policies on Materialized views and streaming tables are supported only when the pipeline owner and the run-as identity are exempt from the policy. When a pipeline refreshes a Materialized view or streaming table, policies are evaluated using the pipeline owner's or run-as identity. If that identity is subject to an ABAC policy, the pipeline refresh fails.

To prevent refresh failures, add the pipeline owner or run-as identity to the `EXCEPT` clause of every ABAC policy applied to the source tables. Use the `TO` clause to specify which users and groups receive masked or filtered data.

Tables with ABAC policies or views that reference tables with ABAC policies can only be shared through OpenSharing if the share owner is exempt from the policy (listed in the `EXCEPT` clause). The policy doesn't govern the recipient's access. Recipients can apply their own ABAC policies to shared tables to enforce access control on their side.

- For share providers, see Add tables and schemas secured by ABAC policies to a share.
- For share recipients, see Read ABAC-secured data and apply ABAC policies.

For details on how to use OpenSharing with ABAC, see OpenSharing and ABAC.

ABAC policies can't be evaluated against historical table snapshots, so time travel queries fail on tables with active row filters or column masks. Deep and shallow clones also aren't supported on tables with ABAC policies.

To enable these operations, create a service principal or group and add it to the policy's `EXCEPT` clause. The policy isn't evaluated for exempted principals, so these operations can run.

Exempted principals see unfiltered, unmasked data. Only exempt trusted identities such as service principals used for ETL or pipeline workloads.

For example, the following policy masks PII columns for all users except the `etl_service_principal`, which can run time travel queries and clone operations:

```
CREATE POLICY mask_pii
ON CATALOG prod
COLUMN MASK prod.governance.mask_value
TO `account users`
EXCEPT `etl_service_principal`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS
  has_tag_value('pii', 'ssn') AS ssn
ON COLUMN ssn;
```

ABAC policies on a source table don't apply to AI Search indexes created from that table. The index syncs all rows from the source table and doesn't enforce row filter or column mask policies when serving queries.

For tables with column masks, you can exclude masked columns from the index using the columns to sync setting.

Only one distinct row filter can resolve at runtime for a given table and a given user, and only one distinct column mask can resolve for a given column and a given user. You can define multiple policies, but when a user queries the table, only one policy's conditions must match. If multiple distinct row filters or column masks apply to the same user and table or column, Databricks blocks access and returns an error. Multiple policies are allowed if they resolve to the same row filter or column mask UDF with the same arguments.

For details, see Rules for multiple filters and masks.

There's no information schema table for ABAC policies. The `information_schema.row_filters` and `information_schema.column_masks` tables show only table-level row filters and column masks. They don't show ABAC policy definitions or the filters and masks derived from ABAC policies at runtime.

To list ABAC policies, use the Unity Catalog REST API. Policy creation, modification, and deletion events are captured in the audit log system table.

For general limitations of row filters and column masks that apply to both ABAC and table-level row filters and column masks, see Limitations.

reference_note.title: ABAC Policies: Key Limitations and Configuration for Databricks Projects
reference_note.summary: ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) policies in Databricks control who sees what data through row filters and column masks. However, they have important limitations: pipeline refreshes fail unless the pipeline owner is exempt, time travel and clones don't work on protected tables, and AI Search indexes ignore the policies. To use ABAC in production, you must add trusted identities to the EXCEPT clause and understand when operations are blocked.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: The EXCEPT clause lists identities (users, groups, service principals) that are NOT subject to the ABAC policy. These exempt identities see all data without filters or masks applied.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: If your pipeline owner or run-as identity is not exempt, pipeline refreshes will fail. You must add them to EXCEPT to keep pipelines working in production.

key_concepts.concept: Row Filters and Column Masks in ABAC
key_concepts.simple_explanation: Row filters hide entire rows from certain users. Column masks hide or transform sensitive column values. Both are defined in ABAC policies and applied at query time based on the user's identity.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: These are the enforcement mechanisms for data governance. Understanding which tables have them helps you predict what data users will see and troubleshoot access issues.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When a user queries a table, Databricks checks the ABAC policy and applies filters or masks based on that user's identity. This happens automatically during query execution.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Policies are enforced dynamically, so you don't need to create separate tables for different users. One table serves everyone with appropriate data visibility.

key_concepts.concept: Only One Policy Can Apply Per User-Table Combination
key_concepts.simple_explanation: For a given user and table, only one row filter can be active. Similarly, only one column mask can be active per column per user. If multiple different policies match, Databricks blocks access with an error.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When designing ABAC policies, you must ensure policies don't conflict. Multiple policies are only allowed if they resolve to the same filter or mask.

important_features_or_tools.name: EXCEPT clause
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which identities are exempt from an ABAC policy. Exempt identities see unfiltered, unmasked data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Always use this for service principals running ETL or pipelines, and for any identity that needs to perform time travel queries or clones on protected tables.

important_features_or_tools.name: TO clause
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which users and groups receive masked or filtered data. This is the target audience for the policy.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this to define who the policy applies to, such as 'account users' or specific groups.

important_features_or_tools.name: COLUMN MASK
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Hides or transforms sensitive column values for users not exempt from the policy. Defined with a masking function and applied to columns matching specific tags.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to protect sensitive data like PII (personally identifiable information) but still allow users to query the table.

important_parameters.meaning: The function that transforms the column value (e.g., prod.governance.mask_value)
Identifies which columns to mask based on tags (e.g., has_tag_value('pii', 'ssn'))

important_features_or_tools.name: Row Filters
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Hides entire rows from users based on conditions. Only rows matching the filter condition are visible to the user.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When different users should see different subsets of rows in the same table (e.g., sales reps see only their region's data).

important_features_or_tools.name: Unity Catalog REST API
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to list, create, modify, and delete ABAC policies programmatically. This is the primary way to manage policies at scale.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to query or manage ABAC policies. The information_schema tables don't show ABAC policy details, so you must use this API.

important_features_or_tools.name: Audit Log System Table
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Captures all policy creation, modification, and deletion events. Provides an audit trail of policy changes.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to track who changed policies and when, for compliance and troubleshooting.

important_features_or_tools.name: OpenSharing with ABAC
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows sharing tables with ABAC policies across Databricks accounts. The share owner must be exempt from the policy. Recipients can apply their own ABAC policies on their side.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When sharing sensitive data with external organizations or other Databricks workspaces while maintaining access control.

important_features_or_tools.name: Columns to Sync Setting
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to exclude masked columns from AI Search indexes. Prevents sensitive data from being indexed.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you have column masks on a table and create an AI Search index, use this to exclude masked columns from the index.

practical_workflow.action: Identify which tables need ABAC policies and what data should be protected (rows or columns).
practical_workflow.reason: You need to know your governance requirements before creating policies. Decide whether you need row filters, column masks, or both.

practical_workflow.action: Create service principals or groups for trusted identities (e.g., ETL pipelines, data engineers) that need to see all data.
practical_workflow.reason: These identities will be added to the EXCEPT clause so they can perform operations like pipeline refreshes, time travel queries, and clones without being blocked.

practical_workflow.action: Create the ABAC policy using CREATE POLICY, specifying the TO clause (target users), EXCEPT clause (exempt identities), and the masking or filtering logic.
practical_workflow.reason: This defines who sees what data. The EXCEPT clause prevents pipeline failures and enables administrative operations.

practical_workflow.action: Test the policy by querying the table as different users to verify filters and masks are applied correctly.
practical_workflow.reason: Policies are evaluated at runtime, so you need to confirm they work as expected before deploying to production.

practical_workflow.action: If using pipelines, ensure the pipeline owner or run-as identity is in the EXCEPT clause of all ABAC policies on source tables.
practical_workflow.reason: Without this exemption, pipeline refreshes will fail because the policy will block the pipeline's access.

practical_workflow.action: If you need time travel queries or clones on protected tables, add the relevant service principal to the EXCEPT clause.
practical_workflow.reason: These operations don't work on tables with active row filters or column masks unless the identity is exempt.

practical_workflow.action: Monitor policy changes using the audit log system table and the Unity Catalog REST API.
practical_workflow.reason: Keeps track of who modified policies and when, important for compliance and troubleshooting access issues.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to add the pipeline owner to the EXCEPT clause, causing pipeline refreshes to fail.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always add the pipeline owner or run-as identity to the EXCEPT clause of every ABAC policy applied to source tables. This is required for pipelines to work.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming time travel queries and clones work on tables with ABAC policies.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Time travel and clones are not supported on tables with active row filters or column masks. You must add the relevant identity to the EXCEPT clause to enable these operations.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking AI Search indexes respect ABAC policies.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: AI Search indexes sync all rows from the source table and ignore row filters and column masks. Use the 'columns to sync' setting to exclude masked columns from the index.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Creating multiple ABAC policies that result in different row filters or column masks for the same user-table combination.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Only one row filter and one column mask can apply per user-table combination. If multiple different policies match, Databricks blocks access. Multiple policies are only allowed if they resolve to the same filter or mask.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Looking for ABAC policy details in information_schema.row_filters or information_schema.column_masks.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: These information_schema tables only show table-level row filters and column masks, not ABAC policies. Use the Unity Catalog REST API to list and manage ABAC policies.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming exempt identities are not trusted and should be limited.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Exempt identities see unfiltered, unmasked data. Only add trusted identities (like ETL service principals) to the EXCEPT clause. Never exempt untrusted users.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking the share recipient's access is governed by the provider's ABAC policy in OpenSharing.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: In OpenSharing, the provider's ABAC policy doesn't govern the recipient's access. Recipients can apply their own ABAC policies to enforce access control on their side.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, always add your ETL or pipeline service principal to the EXCEPT clause of all ABAC policies on source tables. Without this, your data pipelines will fail in production.
If you need to perform time travel queries or clone tables with sensitive data, create a dedicated service principal, add it to the EXCEPT clause, and use it for those operations.
When sharing tables with ABAC policies across accounts using OpenSharing, ensure the share owner is exempt from the policy. The recipient will need to set up their own access controls.
Use the audit log system table to track all ABAC policy changes. This is critical for compliance and debugging access issues in production.
If you use AI Search on tables with column masks, explicitly exclude masked columns using the 'columns to sync' setting to prevent sensitive data from being indexed.
Design ABAC policies carefully to avoid conflicts. Test with multiple user identities before deploying to production to ensure only one policy applies per user-table combination.
Use the Unity Catalog REST API to manage ABAC policies at scale. The information_schema tables don't provide ABAC policy details, so the API is your primary tool for policy management.

source_content:
This tutorial shows how to lock down new tables automatically and release them only after a data steward has reviewed and classified their contents. It uses:

- A schema-level `review_status`control tag so every new table in the schema is masked by default
- Data Classification to automatically detect and tag sensitive columns with `class.*`system tags
- The built-in `system.data_classification.mask_value`function for type-aware masking
- Two policies: one that masks all columns while a table is pending review, and one that masks only classified columns after review

- Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above, or serverless compute.
- Account admin or workspace admin permissions (to create governed tags and enable Data Classification).
- `MANAGE`permission on the target catalog or schema.
- `EXECUTE`on the UDFs.
- A SQL notebook or query editor.

Your organization regularly adds new tables to a Unity Catalog schema from acquisitions, partner integrations, or new product features. By default, any user with `SELECT` on the schema can immediately query new tables, including columns that might contain unclassified PII.

The control tag pattern addresses this: a schema-level `review_status = pending` tag causes every new table in the schema to be fully masked by default. Data Classification scans the table in the background and applies `class.*` tags to detected sensitive columns. After a data steward reviews the classifications and corrects any false positives, they flip `review_status` to `reviewed` at the table level. This overrides the inherited schema tag, and a second policy takes over: masking only the `class.*`-tagged columns while leaving non-sensitive columns accessible.

Data Classification scans tables in the background and applies `class.*` system governed tags such as `class.name`, `class.email_address`, and `class.us_ssn`. No custom tags are required for column-level detection.

- In Catalog Explorer, select your catalog and go to the **Details**tab.
- Next to **Data Classification**, click**Enable**.
- Optionally choose which schemas to include.

Automatic tagging is enabled later, from the Data Classification results page after reviewing initial detections (Step 6).

For full details, see Data Classification.

Create the following governed tag in the Catalog Explorer UI (**Catalog** > **Govern** > **Governed Tags** > **Create governed tag**):

| Tag key | Allowed values |
|---|---|
|
 |
 |

Tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally. Do not use tag names, values, or descriptors that could compromise the security of your resources. For example, do not use tag names, values or descriptors that contain personal or sensitive information.

Create a schema and set the control tag to `pending`. Every table created in this schema inherits this tag automatically.

```
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS abac_tutorial;
USE CATALOG abac_tutorial;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS secure_default;
ALTER SCHEMA abac_tutorial.secure_default
  SET TAGS ('review_status' = 'pending');
```

When a table has `review_status = pending`, all columns are masked. `MATCH COLUMNS TRUE` matches every column regardless of tags.

`system.data_classification.mask_value` is a type-aware masking function provided by Databricks. It returns a safe placeholder based on the runtime data type. For example, it returns `0` for integers, `DATE '1970-01-01'` for dates, and a SHA-256 hash for strings. No custom UDF is needed.

```
CREATE POLICY review_pending_policy
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.secure_default
COLUMN MASK system.data_classification.mask_value
TO `account users`
FOR TABLES
WHEN has_tag_value('review_status', 'pending')
MATCH COLUMNS TRUE AS m ON COLUMN m;
```
To exempt specific groups from the policy, add an `EXCEPT` clause. For example, `TO \`account users` EXCEPT `data_admins``lets members of the`data_admins` group bypass the mask and see unmasked data.

reference_note.title: Automatic Table Lockdown and Review Workflow with Data Classification
reference_note.summary: Learn how to automatically mask new tables in Unity Catalog until a data steward reviews and classifies them. This tutorial uses schema-level control tags, Databricks Data Classification to detect sensitive columns, and column-level masking policies to ensure PII is protected by default. New tables are fully masked until marked as reviewed, then only classified sensitive columns remain masked.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A tag applied at the schema level (like `review_status = pending`) that automatically applies to all new tables in that schema. It acts as a default security setting for the entire schema.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Ensures every new table is secure by default without manual intervention. Prevents accidental exposure of unclassified PII when new tables are added.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A Databricks feature that automatically scans tables in the background and detects sensitive data (like names, emails, SSNs). It tags detected columns with system tags like `class.name`, `class.email_address`, `class.us_ssn`.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Removes the manual burden of identifying sensitive columns. Enables automated, intelligent masking policies based on actual data content rather than guessing.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that hides or transforms column values based on conditions (like tags or user roles). Different policies can apply depending on the table's review status.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Allows fine-grained control over who sees what data. Non-sensitive columns remain accessible while sensitive ones are protected.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Custom metadata tags you create and control in Databricks. They have a key (like `review_status`) and allowed values (like `pending` or `reviewed`).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Provides a standardized way to label resources and trigger policies. Ensures consistent security rules across your catalog.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Masking that returns appropriate placeholder values based on the column's data type (e.g., `0` for integers, `DATE '1970-01-01'` for dates, SHA-256 hash for strings).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Prevents errors when masked data is used in calculations or comparisons. Queries don't break because masked values match the expected data type.

important_features_or_tools.name: Data Classification
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Automatically scans tables and detects sensitive data columns, applying system-generated `class.*` tags like `class.name`, `class.email_address`, `class.us_ssn`.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Enable this on your catalog to automatically identify PII and sensitive columns without manual tagging. Run it before setting up masking policies.

important_parameters.meaning: Choose which schemas to include in Data Classification scans

important_features_or_tools.name: Governed Tags
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Custom metadata tags you create in Catalog Explorer with specific allowed values. Can be applied to catalogs, schemas, tables, and columns.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Create a `review_status` governed tag with values `pending` and `reviewed` to control the masking workflow.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the tag (e.g., `review_status`)
The specific values this tag can have (e.g., `pending`, `reviewed`)

important_features_or_tools.name: system.data_classification.mask_value
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Built-in Databricks function that masks column values with type-appropriate placeholders. Returns `0` for integers, `DATE '1970-01-01'` for dates, SHA-256 hash for strings.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this in column masking policies instead of writing custom UDFs. It handles type conversion automatically.

important_features_or_tools.name: Column Masking Policy (CREATE POLICY)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Defines a rule that masks specific columns based on conditions like tags or user roles. Applied automatically when conditions are met.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Create two policies: one for `review_status = pending` (mask all columns), one for `review_status = reviewed` (mask only `class.*`-tagged columns).

important_parameters.meaning: Specifies the masking function to apply (e.g., `system.data_classification.mask_value`)
Specifies which users or groups the policy applies to (e.g., `account users`)
Exempts specific groups from the policy (e.g., `EXCEPT `data_admins``)
Condition that triggers the policy (e.g., `has_tag_value('review_status', 'pending')`)
`TRUE` matches all columns; can also match specific tags like `has_tag_value('class.*')`

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Databricks UI for managing catalogs, schemas, tables, and governance settings. Access Data Classification, Governed Tags, and tag management here.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use to enable Data Classification, create governed tags, and review classification results.

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER SCHEMA SET TAGS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Applies a tag to a schema so all new tables in that schema inherit the tag automatically.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Set `review_status = pending` on your schema to ensure all new tables are masked by default.

important_parameters.meaning: The tag key-value pair to apply (e.g., `'review_status' = 'pending'`)

practical_workflow.action: Verify you have the required permissions: Account admin or workspace admin (to create governed tags and enable Data Classification), `MANAGE` on the target catalog/schema, and `EXECUTE` on UDFs.
practical_workflow.reason: You cannot proceed without these permissions. Check with your Databricks administrator if you lack any.

practical_workflow.action: Enable Data Classification on your catalog. In Catalog Explorer, select your catalog, go to the **Details** tab, and click **Enable** next to **Data Classification**. Optionally choose which schemas to include.
practical_workflow.reason: Data Classification must be enabled before it can scan tables and detect sensitive columns.

practical_workflow.action: Create a governed tag in Catalog Explorer (**Catalog** > **Govern** > **Governed Tags** > **Create governed tag**). Create a tag with key `review_status` and allowed values `pending` and `reviewed`.
practical_workflow.reason: This tag controls the masking workflow. It signals whether a table has been reviewed and classified.

practical_workflow.action: Create a schema and set the control tag to `pending`. Run: `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS secure_default; ALTER SCHEMA abac_tutorial.secure_default SET TAGS ('review_status' = 'pending');`
practical_workflow.reason: All new tables in this schema will inherit `review_status = pending` and be fully masked by default.

practical_workflow.action: Create the first masking policy for pending tables. Use `CREATE POLICY review_pending_policy` with `WHEN has_tag_value('review_status', 'pending')` and `MATCH COLUMNS TRUE` to mask all columns.
practical_workflow.reason: This policy ensures all columns are masked while a table awaits review, protecting unclassified PII.

practical_workflow.action: Wait for Data Classification to scan new tables in the background. Review the classification results in the Data Classification results page. Correct any false positives.
practical_workflow.reason: Data Classification detects sensitive columns and tags them with `class.*` tags. You must review and approve these before enabling automatic tagging.

practical_workflow.action: After reviewing classifications, enable automatic tagging from the Data Classification results page.
practical_workflow.reason: This allows Data Classification to automatically tag detected sensitive columns going forward.

practical_workflow.action: Create the second masking policy for reviewed tables. Use `CREATE POLICY` with `WHEN has_tag_value('review_status', 'reviewed')` and `MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('class.*')` to mask only classified columns.
practical_workflow.reason: After review, only truly sensitive columns (tagged with `class.*`) remain masked. Non-sensitive columns become accessible.

practical_workflow.action: When a data steward has reviewed a table and confirmed classifications are correct, change the table's tag from `review_status = pending` to `review_status = reviewed`.
practical_workflow.reason: This triggers the second policy, which masks only classified columns and allows access to non-sensitive data.

practical_workflow.action: Optionally add an `EXCEPT` clause to your policies to exempt specific groups (e.g., `data_admins`) from masking.
practical_workflow.reason: Data stewards and admins need to see unmasked data to review and classify columns. This allows them to bypass the mask.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking Data Classification happens instantly. It scans tables in the background, so there may be a delay before sensitive columns are detected and tagged.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Plan for a review period after enabling Data Classification. Check the Data Classification results page to see when scans complete and review the detected tags before enabling automatic tagging.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Creating custom tags for column classification instead of using the built-in `class.*` system tags.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use the system-generated `class.*` tags that Data Classification creates automatically (e.g., `class.name`, `class.email_address`). No custom tags are needed for column-level detection.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Applying the `review_status` tag only to tables instead of the schema.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Apply `review_status = pending` to the schema so all new tables inherit it automatically. This ensures every new table is masked by default without manual intervention.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using a custom masking function instead of `system.data_classification.mask_value`.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use the built-in `system.data_classification.mask_value` function. It handles type-aware masking automatically and returns appropriate placeholders for each data type.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to exempt data stewards or admins from masking policies, so they cannot see unmasked data to review classifications.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Add an `EXCEPT` clause to your policies to allow specific groups (like `data_admins`) to bypass the mask and see unmasked data for review purposes.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Including sensitive information (like PII) in tag names, values, or descriptors.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally. Use generic, non-sensitive names like `review_status`, not names that reveal what data is protected.

project_usage_notes: This workflow is ideal for organizations that frequently add new tables from acquisitions, partner integrations, or new product features. It prevents accidental PII exposure by masking all new tables by default.

The two-policy approach (pending vs. reviewed) creates a clear workflow: new tables are fully masked, Data Classification detects sensitive columns, a steward reviews and approves, then only truly sensitive columns remain masked.
Use the `EXCEPT` clause in policies to create a data steward role that can see unmasked data for review and classification purposes, while regular users see masked data.
Requires Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above, or serverless compute. Verify your workspace meets this requirement before starting.

The `review_status` tag is a control tag that overrides schema-level inheritance when set at the table level. This allows fine-grained control: schema default is `pending`, but individual tables can be marked `reviewed` after steward approval.
Data Classification scans run in the background and may take time. Plan your review workflow with this delay in mind. Check the Data Classification results page regularly to see progress.

This pattern works best when combined with role-based access control (RBAC). Ensure data stewards have `MANAGE` permissions on the catalog/schema and are exempted from masking policies so they can perform reviews.

  (4, 'David Lee',      'david.lee@gmail.com',  '456-78-9012', '555-0404', 'Houston Floor 2',    'Marketing Lead',      'Growth'),
  (5, 'Eva Martinez',   'eva.m@hotmail.com',    '567-89-0123', '555-0505', 'Phoenix Building B', 'HR Business Partner', 'People');
```
Run the following query to confirm that all columns are masked.

```
SELECT * FROM abac_tutorial.secure_default.employee_directory;
```

Once Data Classification scans the table (within 24 hours of enabling it), review the detections and enable auto tagging so that `class.*` tags are applied to both existing and future detections.

- In Catalog Explorer, select your catalog and go to the **Details**tab.
- Next to **Data Classification**, click**View results**.
- Review the detections and provide feedback on any mistakes by clicking the **Exclude**icon next to incorrect detections.
- Enable automatic tagging for the classification tags you want applied. Tags populate in the next scan (within 24 hours).

For details on the Data Classification UI and automatic tagging, see View classification results and Enable automatic tagging.

For this tutorial, run the following to simulate the `class.*` tags that auto tagging would apply, so you can see the end-to-end flow without waiting for a background scan.

```
-- Simulate Data Classification tags (in production, these are applied automatically)
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.secure_default.employee_directory
  ALTER COLUMN full_name SET TAGS ('class.name' = '');
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.secure_default.employee_directory
  ALTER COLUMN personal_email SET TAGS ('class.email_address' = '');
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.secure_default.employee_directory
  ALTER COLUMN ssn_number SET TAGS ('class.us_ssn' = '');
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.secure_default.employee_directory
  ALTER COLUMN phone SET TAGS ('class.phone_number' = '');
```

When a table is marked as `reviewed`, only columns tagged with `class.*` tags are masked. Non-classified columns become visible.

```
CREATE POLICY review_complete_policy
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.secure_default
COLUMN MASK system.data_classification.mask_value
TO `account users`
FOR TABLES
WHEN has_tag_value('review_status', 'reviewed')
MATCH COLUMNS (
  has_tag('class.name')
  OR has_tag('class.email_address')
  OR has_tag('class.us_ssn')
  OR has_tag('class.phone_number')
  OR has_tag('class.credit_card')
  OR has_tag('class.date_of_birth')
) AS m
ON COLUMN m;
```

Mark the table as reviewed. The table-level `reviewed` tag overrides the inherited schema-level `pending` tag, so the pending policy no longer applies and the reviewed policy takes over.

```
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.secure_default.employee_directory
  SET TAGS ('review_status' = 'reviewed');
```
Run the following query to confirm the change. Columns with `class.*` tags (`full_name`, `personal_email`, `ssn_number`, `phone`) remain masked. Non-classified columns (`id`, `office_location`, `title`, `team`) are now visible.

```
SELECT * FROM abac_tutorial.secure_default.employee_directory;
```

reference_note.title: Creating and Masking Tables with Data Classification and ABAC Policies
reference_note.summary: Learn how to create a table that automatically inherits masking policies from its schema, use Data Classification to identify sensitive columns, apply classification tags, and then create attribute-based access control (ABAC) policies that mask only classified columns. This workflow ensures sensitive data like SSNs and emails are protected while allowing access to non-sensitive columns.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When you create a table in a schema that has tags (like `review_status = pending`), the table automatically inherits those tags. This means policies attached to the schema apply to the table immediately.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In a real project, this lets you set up masking policies once at the schema level and have them automatically protect all new tables you create, without needing to configure each table individually.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks automatically scans your tables to detect sensitive data types (like SSNs, emails, phone numbers) and tags the columns with classification tags like `class.us_ssn` or `class.email_address`.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This saves time by automatically identifying which columns contain sensitive data, so you don't have to manually tag every sensitive column yourself.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Tags that Databricks applies to columns to indicate what type of sensitive data they contain, such as `class.name`, `class.email_address`, `class.us_ssn`, `class.phone_number`, `class.credit_card`, or `class.date_of_birth`.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: These tags are used in masking policies to decide which columns should be masked. You can create one policy that masks all columns with any `class.*` tag, rather than writing separate policies for each column.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Policies that use tags and conditions to automatically mask or restrict data. Instead of saying 'mask this specific column,' you say 'mask any column that has a `class.email_address` tag AND the table has `review_status = reviewed`.'
key_concepts.why_it_matters: ABAC policies are flexible and scalable. As you add new tables and columns, the same policy automatically applies to them if they have the right tags, without needing to update the policy.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When a table has its own tag (like `review_status = reviewed`), it overrides the inherited tag from the schema (like `review_status = pending`). This allows different policies to apply based on the table's review status.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In a real project, this lets you have different masking rules for tables that have been reviewed and approved versus tables that are still pending review.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a new table in a specified schema. If the table already exists, it replaces it. The table automatically inherits any tags from its schema.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to create a new table and have it inherit masking policies from the schema.

important_parameters.meaning: The full path to the table (catalog.schema.table)

important_features_or_tools.name: Data Classification
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks feature that automatically scans tables to detect sensitive data types and applies classification tags to columns. Scans run within 24 hours of being enabled.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Enable this on your catalog to automatically identify and tag sensitive columns without manual effort.

important_parameters.meaning: Data Classification scans run automatically within 24 hours of enabling the feature

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer > Details tab > View results
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Shows you the results of Data Classification scans, including which columns were detected as sensitive and what classification tags were applied. You can review detections, exclude incorrect ones, and enable automatic tagging.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: After Data Classification scans your table, use this to review the detections and decide which classification tags should be automatically applied to future columns.

important_parameters.meaning: Click this to mark a detection as incorrect and prevent that classification from being applied
Turn on automatic tagging for specific classification tags so they are applied to both existing and future columns

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Manually applies tags to a specific column. Used to simulate or set classification tags on columns.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to manually tag columns (for testing) or when automatic tagging hasn't run yet.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the column to tag
The tag to apply, typically in the format `class.data_type`

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE POLICY
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates an attribute-based access control (ABAC) policy that masks or restricts data based on tags and conditions. Policies can apply to schemas, tables, or specific columns.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to set up automatic masking rules that apply to multiple tables based on their tags.

important_parameters.meaning: Specifies that this policy masks column values
A built-in masking function that replaces sensitive values with a masked representation
Applies the policy to all account users
Specifies that this policy applies to tables
Condition that checks if a table has a specific tag with a specific value
Specifies which columns the policy applies to based on their tags

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER TABLE ... SET TAGS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Sets a tag on a table (not a column). Used to mark a table's review status or other attributes.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to change a table's tag (e.g., from `review_status = pending` to `review_status = reviewed`) to trigger different policies.

important_parameters.meaning: The tag to set on the table
The value of the tag

important_features_or_tools.name: SELECT * query
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Queries the table to see which columns are masked and which are visible based on the active policies.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: After creating or modifying policies, run this to verify that masking is working as expected.

practical_workflow.action: Create a table in a schema that has a `review_status = pending` tag
practical_workflow.reason: The table automatically inherits the pending tag, which triggers a masking policy that masks all columns by default.

practical_workflow.action: Insert data into the table and run a SELECT query to confirm all columns are masked
practical_workflow.reason: This verifies that the inherited policy is working and all sensitive data is protected.

practical_workflow.action: Enable Data Classification on your catalog and wait for it to scan the table (within 24 hours)
practical_workflow.reason: Data Classification automatically detects sensitive columns and applies classification tags like `class.us_ssn` and `class.email_address`.

practical_workflow.action: Review the Data Classification results in Catalog Explorer and enable automatic tagging for the classification tags you want applied
practical_workflow.reason: This ensures that all sensitive columns are properly tagged so policies can identify them.

practical_workflow.action: Create an ABAC policy that masks only columns with `class.*` tags when the table has `review_status = reviewed`
practical_workflow.reason: This policy allows non-sensitive columns to become visible once a table is marked as reviewed, while keeping sensitive columns masked.

practical_workflow.action: Mark the table as reviewed by setting `review_status = reviewed` on the table
practical_workflow.reason: This table-level tag overrides the inherited schema-level tag, so the reviewed policy takes over and only columns with `class.*` tags remain masked.

practical_workflow.action: Run a SELECT query to confirm that classified columns are masked and non-classified columns are visible
practical_workflow.reason: This verifies that the policy is working correctly and the right columns are protected.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that all columns will remain masked even after marking a table as reviewed
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: When a table is marked as `review_status = reviewed`, only columns with `class.*` tags remain masked. Non-classified columns become visible. The reviewed policy is more granular than the pending policy.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Waiting for Data Classification to scan before you can test masking policies
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You can manually apply classification tags using `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS` to simulate the tags that Data Classification would apply. This lets you test policies without waiting 24 hours.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that a table-level tag and a schema-level tag both apply at the same time
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: When a table has its own tag, it overrides the inherited schema-level tag. Only one value applies at a time. This is how you can have different policies for different tables.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Creating separate masking policies for each sensitive data type
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use ABAC policies with tag-based conditions (like `has_tag('class.email_address') OR has_tag('class.us_ssn')`) to create one policy that applies to all sensitive columns, regardless of type.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, set up a schema with `review_status = pending` and attach a masking policy to it. All new tables created in that schema will automatically be masked until you review them and mark them as `review_status = reviewed`.
Enable Data Classification on your catalog early so that sensitive columns are automatically tagged. This saves time and reduces the risk of missing sensitive data.

Use the reviewed policy to allow business users to see non-sensitive columns (like office location, title, team) while keeping sensitive columns (like SSN, email, phone) masked. This balances security with usability.
Test your policies by running SELECT queries after each step. This helps you catch configuration errors early and understand exactly which columns are masked and why.

If you have multiple sensitive data types (SSN, credit card, date of birth, etc.), use a single ABAC policy with OR conditions to mask all of them at once. This is easier to maintain than separate policies for each type.

reference_note.title: Creating Tables with Inherited Security Policies in Databricks
reference_note.summary: When you create a new table in a schema with an existing security policy, the table automatically inherits that policy without needing extra configuration. New tables start with review_status = pending and are fully locked down. You can verify masking is working by querying the table, and masking behavior changes once Data Classification tags columns and review_status changes to reviewed.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When you create a table in a schema that already has a security policy attached, the new table automatically gets that same policy applied. You don't need to manually configure anything.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This saves time and ensures consistent security across all tables in a schema. Every new table is protected by default without extra steps.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: This is the default state for new tables. It means the table is fully masked and locked down until a Data Classification scan reviews the columns and marks them with tags.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: It ensures new tables are secure by default. Data is hidden until someone explicitly reviews and classifies what columns should be visible.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A Data Classification scan examines your table columns and applies tags (like class.*) to them. These tags determine which columns stay masked and which become visible when review_status changes to reviewed.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tagging controls which sensitive data remains protected and which data can be shown to different users based on their access level.

practical_workflow.reason: The table automatically inherits the policy (review_status = pending) without extra configuration

practical_workflow.reason: You need data in the table to verify that masking policies are working correctly

practical_workflow.reason: This verifies that the inherited policy is actively masking sensitive data

practical_workflow.reason: Tagging determines which columns will remain masked vs. visible when review_status changes to reviewed

practical_workflow.action: When done, use DROP commands to remove tables, policies, schemas, and catalogs in the correct order
practical_workflow.reason: Proper cleanup prevents orphaned objects and keeps your Databricks workspace organized

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking you need to manually apply a policy to each new table in a schema
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Policies are inherited automatically by all tables in a schema. No manual configuration needed for each table.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Expecting all columns to remain masked forever
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Columns only stay masked if they are tagged with class.* tags by Data Classification. Untagged columns become visible when review_status changes to reviewed.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to drop a schema without using CASCADE when it contains tables
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always use CASCADE when dropping a schema with tables, or drop the tables first individually.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to remove governed tags when cleaning up
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use the Catalog Explorer UI to manually remove governed tags like review_status after dropping all related objects.

project_usage_notes: When building a real project, create tables in a schema with existing security policies to get automatic protection without extra work.
Always verify masking is working by running a SELECT query after creating a new table with inherited policies.
Plan for Data Classification scans to run on your tables so that column tagging happens and masking behavior is properly configured.
When cleaning up a project, follow the correct order: drop policies first, then tables, then schemas, then catalogs. Use the Catalog Explorer UI to remove any remaining governed tags.
Use review_status = pending as a safe default for new tables until you're ready to review and classify columns.

source_content:
This tutorial shows you how to configure row filter and column mask attribute-based access control (ABAC) policies in Unity Catalog using the Catalog Explorer UI. For a fully SQL-based version that also covers conditional email masking, see Tutorial: Configure ABAC with SQL.

In this example, a US analytics team should not be able to access EU customer records or SSNs. However, they should be able to access other customers and customer data in the same table. This tutorial includes the following steps:

- Create a governed tag
- Create a Unity Catalog catalog, schema, and table
- Apply governed tags to columns
- Create a UDF for hiding EU member's data
- Create a row filter policy
- Create a UDF for hiding SSNs
- Create a column mask policy
- Select your table using the policies

For a demo of configuring ABAC, see Discover Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) with Unity Catalog.

- Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above, or serverless compute.
- Account admin or workspace admin permissions (to create governed tags).
- To apply governed tags to columns (Step 3): the `ASSIGN`privilege on the governed tag (account admins have this by default) and the`APPLY TAG`privilege on the target table.
- `MANAGE`permission on the target catalog or schema.
- `EXECUTE`on the UDFs.

Compute running older runtimes cannot access tables secured by ABAC. As a temporary workaround, you can configure ABAC to apply only to a specific group. Add the users you want to restrict to that group. Users who are not in the group can still access the tables.

To create a governed tag, you must have the governed tag CREATE permission at the account level. Account and workspace admins have CREATE by default.

-
In your Databricks workspace, click **Catalog**.
-
Click the **Govern**button.
-
In the dropdown menu, click **Governed Tags**.
-
Click **Create governed tag**.
-
Enter the tag key `pii`.
-
Enter a description for the governed tag.
-
Enter the allowed values for the tag: `ssn`and`address`. Only these values can be assigned to this tag key.
-
Click **Create**.

Tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally. Do not use tag names, values, or descriptors that could compromise the security of your resources. For example, do not use tag names, values or descriptors that contain personal or sensitive information.

To follow these steps, you must have the `CREATE CATALOG` permission on your Unity Catalog metastore. You can also create the table in a schema that you have the `CREATE TABLE` permission on.

- In the sidebar, click **+New**>**Notebook**.
- Select `SQL`as your notebook language.
- Click **Connect**and attach the notebook to a compute resource.
- Add the following commands to the notebook and run them:

```
-- Create catalog (if not already exists)
CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS abac;
USE CATALOG abac;
-- Create schema
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS customers;
USE SCHEMA customers;
-- Create table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS profiles (
    First_Name STRING,
    Last_Name STRING,
    Phone_Number STRING,
    Address STRING,
    SSN STRING
)
USING DELTA;
-- Insert data
INSERT INTO profiles (First_Name, Last_Name, Phone_Number, Address, SSN)
VALUES
('John', 'Doe', '123-456-7890', '123 Main St, NY', '123-45-6789'),
('Jane', 'Smith', '234-567-8901', '456 Oak St, CA', '234-56-7890'),
('Alice', 'Johnson', '345-678-9012', '789 Pine St, TX', '345-67-8901'),
('Bob', 'Brown', '456-789-0123', '321 Maple St, FL', '456-78-9012'),
('Charlie', 'Davis', '567-890-1234', '654 Cedar St, IL', '567-89-0123'),
('Emily', 'White', '678-901-2345', '987 Birch St, WA', '678-90-1234'),
('Frank', 'Miller', '789-012-3456', '741 Spruce St, WA', '789-01-2345'),
('Grace', 'Wilson', '890-123-4567', '852 Elm St, NV', '890-12-3456'),
('Hank', 'Moore', '901-234-5678', '963 Walnut St, CO', '901-23-4567'),
('Ivy', 'Taylor', '012-345-6789', '159 Aspen St, AZ', '012-34-5678'),
('Liam', 'Connor', '111-222-3333', '12 Abbey Street, Dublin, Ireland EU', '111-22-3333'),
('Sophie', 'Dubois', '222-333-4444', '45 Rue de Rivoli, Paris, France Europe', '222-33-4444'),

reference_note.title: Configure Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) with Row Filters and Column Masks in Unity Catalog
reference_note.summary: ABAC lets you control which rows and columns specific users can see in a table based on governed tags and policies. In this tutorial, you'll create governed tags, apply them to table columns, and use User-Defined Functions (UDFs) with row filter and column mask policies to restrict a US analytics team from seeing EU customer records and SSNs. This is useful when different teams need access to the same table but should only see specific data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Labels you create at the account level that can be applied to table columns to mark what kind of data they contain (e.g., 'pii' tag with values 'ssn' or 'address'). Only the values you define can be assigned to a tag.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Governed tags are the foundation of ABAC—they identify which columns contain sensitive data so policies can protect them

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that hides entire rows from certain users based on conditions. For example, hide all rows where the address contains 'EU' from the US analytics team.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Prevents users from seeing data they shouldn't access, even if they can connect to the table

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that hides or transforms the content of specific columns for certain users. For example, show '***' instead of the actual SSN value.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Protects sensitive data in columns (like SSNs) by replacing it with masked values instead of removing the column entirely

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Custom SQL functions you write to define the logic for what data to hide or mask. For example, a UDF that checks if an address contains 'EU' or 'Europe'.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: UDFs give you flexible control over exactly which rows or values to filter or mask based on your business rules

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks' centralized metadata and governance system where you organize data into catalogs, schemas, and tables, and apply security policies.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: ABAC policies are applied through Unity Catalog, so you need to understand the catalog → schema → table hierarchy

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer UI
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A visual interface in Databricks where you can create and manage governed tags, apply tags to columns, and configure ABAC policies without writing SQL
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want a UI-based approach to setting up ABAC (alternative to SQL-based configuration)

important_features_or_tools.name: Govern > Governed Tags
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: The section in Catalog Explorer where you create new governed tags at the account level
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: First step in setting up ABAC—create your tags before applying them to columns

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the tag (e.g., 'pii')
The only values that can be assigned to this tag key (e.g., 'ssn', 'address')
A description of what the tag is used for

important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: SQL command to create a new catalog in Unity Catalog
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When setting up a new workspace or project area for your data

important_parameters.meaning: Optional clause to avoid errors if the catalog already exists

important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: To organize related tables within a catalog

important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: SQL command to create a new Delta table with specified columns and data types
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to create a table to hold data that will be protected by ABAC policies

important_parameters.meaning: Specifies that the table uses Delta Lake format (Databricks' default storage format)

important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: SQL command to add rows of data to a table
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When populating a table with test or production data

important_features_or_tools.name: Row Filter Policy
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A policy that uses a UDF to determine which rows a user can see based on conditions
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to hide entire rows from certain users (e.g., hide EU customer records from US team)

important_parameters.meaning: The function that evaluates whether a row should be visible to the user

important_features_or_tools.name: Column Mask Policy
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A policy that uses a UDF to replace or hide the values in specific columns for certain users
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to hide sensitive data in a column (e.g., mask SSNs with '***') while keeping the column visible

important_parameters.meaning: The function that transforms the column value (e.g., returns '***' instead of the actual SSN)

important_features_or_tools.name: ASSIGN privilege
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Permission required to assign governed tag values to columns
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Account admins have this by default; others need it to apply tags to columns

important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Permission required to apply a governed tag to a table or column
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Needed to mark columns with governed tags as part of ABAC setup

important_features_or_tools.name: MANAGE permission
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Permission required to manage policies on a catalog or schema
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Needed to create and configure row filter and column mask policies

important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Needed for users who will be subject to ABAC policies that use UDFs

practical_workflow.action: Create a governed tag in Catalog Explorer (Govern > Governed Tags > Create governed tag). Set the tag key (e.g., 'pii') and define allowed values (e.g., 'ssn', 'address').
practical_workflow.reason: Governed tags are the foundation of ABAC—they label which columns contain sensitive data

practical_workflow.action: Create a Unity Catalog, schema, and table using SQL commands (CREATE CATALOG, CREATE SCHEMA, CREATE TABLE) in a SQL notebook
practical_workflow.reason: You need a table to apply ABAC policies to; organizing it in a catalog and schema makes it easier to manage

practical_workflow.action: Apply governed tags to columns in the table using Catalog Explorer (e.g., tag the 'SSN' column with 'pii=ssn')
practical_workflow.reason: Tagging columns tells Databricks which columns are sensitive and need protection

practical_workflow.action: Create a UDF that defines the logic for hiding rows (e.g., a function that checks if an address contains 'EU' or 'Europe')
practical_workflow.reason: The UDF is the engine that decides which rows to filter based on your business rules

practical_workflow.action: Create a row filter policy in Catalog Explorer that applies the UDF to the table
practical_workflow.reason: The policy enforces the row filtering rule—users matching the policy conditions will only see rows the UDF allows

practical_workflow.reason: The UDF transforms sensitive values so users see masked data instead of the real values

practical_workflow.reason: The policy enforces the masking rule—users matching the policy conditions will see masked values in that column

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using sensitive information (like personal names or SSNs) in tag names, values, or descriptions
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally. Use generic, non-sensitive names like 'pii', 'ssn', 'address' instead

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that ABAC policies apply to all users automatically
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: ABAC policies apply only to users on compute running Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above (or serverless compute). Older runtimes cannot access ABAC-protected tables. As a workaround, you can configure policies to apply only to specific groups

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing row filters with column masks
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Row filters hide entire rows from users; column masks hide or transform values within columns. Use row filters to restrict which records users see, and column masks to hide sensitive data within visible records

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to grant the required permissions before setting up ABAC
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You need: account/workspace admin for creating governed tags, ASSIGN and APPLY TAG privileges for tagging columns, MANAGE permission for creating policies, and EXECUTE permission for UDFs

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Creating UDFs without understanding the business logic needed
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Before writing a UDF, clearly define what data should be hidden or masked and for which users. The UDF is just the implementation of that logic

project_usage_notes: In a real project, use ABAC when multiple teams need access to the same table but should see different data. Example: US and EU teams accessing a customer table where EU team sees all data but US team cannot see EU customer records or SSNs.
Start by identifying which columns contain sensitive data (PII, financial data, etc.) and tag them with governed tags. This makes it easy to apply consistent policies across multiple tables.
Write UDFs that reflect your actual business rules. For example, if you need to hide data based on geography, customer segment, or data classification, encode that logic in the UDF.
Test ABAC policies with different user groups before deploying to production. Verify that each group sees only the data they should have access to.
Remember that ABAC requires Databricks Runtime 16.4+ or serverless compute. If your organization uses older runtimes, plan a compute upgrade or use the group-based workaround.
Document your governed tags, UDFs, and policies so other team members understand what data is protected and why. This is important for compliance and auditing.

```
-- Add the governed tag to ssn column
ALTER TABLE abac.customers.profiles
ALTER COLUMN SSN
SET TAGS ('pii' = 'ssn');
-- Add governed tag to address column
ALTER TABLE abac.customers.profiles
ALTER COLUMN Address
SET TAGS ('pii' = 'address');
```

- Add the following command to the notebook and run it:

```
-- Determine if an address is not in the EU
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION is_not_eu_address(address STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN (
    SELECT CASE
        WHEN LOWER(address) LIKE '%eu%'
          OR LOWER(address) LIKE '%e.u.%'
          OR LOWER(address) LIKE '%europe%'
        THEN FALSE
        ELSE TRUE
    END
);
```
This UDF checks whether a given string does not appear to reference Europe or the EU. If any of these substrings are found, it returns FALSE (meaning it is an EU address). If none of the substrings are found, it returns TRUE (meaning it is not an EU address).
