reference_note.title: Creating Row-Level Access Control Policies with Tags and UDFs in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Learn how to use Databricks attribute-based access control (ABAC) to automatically hide table rows based on conditions. You'll tag sensitive columns, create a user-defined function (UDF) to define the hiding logic, then build a policy that applies the function to control who sees which rows. This ensures data governance without manually managing access for each user.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Labels you attach to specific columns in a table to mark them as sensitive or special. In this example, the 'pii' tag marks columns containing personally identifiable information.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tags let you group columns by purpose so policies can automatically apply to all columns with the same tag, rather than managing each column individually.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A custom function you write in SQL that returns TRUE or FALSE. The UDF evaluates data and decides whether a row should be hidden or shown based on your business logic.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: UDFs let you encode complex business rules (like 'hide EU addresses') once, then reuse them in multiple policies without duplicating logic.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that automatically hides or shows entire rows of data based on a condition, applied to specific users or groups. The policy uses your UDF to decide which rows to hide.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Policies enforce data governance automatically—users see only the rows they're allowed to see, without manual row-by-row access management.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A security model where access decisions are based on attributes (like tags on columns) and conditions (like a UDF result), rather than hardcoding which users can access which data.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: ABAC scales better than manual access lists—as your data grows, policies automatically apply to new columns and rows without reconfiguration.

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Adds a tag to a specific column in a table. Tags are key-value pairs (e.g., 'pii' = 'ssn') that label columns for governance purposes.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to mark columns as sensitive, regulated, or special so policies can reference them by tag instead of by column name.

important_parameters.meaning: The full path to the table (catalog.schema.table)
The column to tag
The tag key and value to assign

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a user-defined function (UDF) in SQL that takes input parameters and returns a result. In this case, the function checks if an address is not in the EU and returns TRUE or FALSE.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to encode business logic (like 'is this address in Europe?') that will be reused in policies or queries.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the function and the type of input it accepts
The data type the function returns
The logic that determines what the function returns

important_features_or_tools.name: Policies Tab in Catalog
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A section in the Databricks UI where you create and manage row-level and column-level access control policies for a catalog.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to set up automated data governance rules that control which rows or columns users can see.

important_features_or_tools.name: New Policy Dialog
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A form in the Databricks UI where you define a policy by setting its name, scope, principals, conditions, and the function it uses.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Every time you want to create a new access control policy.

important_parameters.meaning: A unique identifier for the policy
A human-readable explanation of what the policy does
The principals (users or groups) the policy applies to
Principals to exclude from the policy (optional)
The catalog and schemas where the policy applies
The type of policy: 'Hide table rows' or 'Hide columns'

important_features_or_tools.name: Select existing function in Policy Conditions
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to choose a UDF from Unity Catalog to define the condition for hiding rows. The UDF's TRUE/FALSE result determines whether a row is hidden.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want a policy to use a custom function to decide which rows to hide.

important_parameters.meaning: The catalog, schema, and function name (must be in Unity Catalog)

important_features_or_tools.name: Map column to parameter if it has a specific tag
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Tells the policy to automatically pass the value of any column with a specific tag to the UDF as a parameter. The policy finds columns with the tag and feeds their values to the function.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want the policy to apply the UDF to all columns with a certain tag (e.g., all columns tagged 'pii : address').

important_parameters.meaning: The tag key and value to search for (e.g., 'pii : address')

important_features_or_tools.name: Test function (optional)

important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Before finalizing a policy, to ensure your UDF logic is correct.

important_parameters.meaning: A sample value to pass to the UDF

practical_workflow.action: Tag sensitive columns in your table using ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS. For example, tag the SSN column with 'pii' = 'ssn' and the Address column with 'pii' = 'address'.
practical_workflow.reason: Tags identify which columns are sensitive so policies can reference them by tag rather than by individual column name. This makes policies reusable across multiple columns.

practical_workflow.action: Create a UDF using CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION that encodes your business logic. The UDF should return TRUE or FALSE based on whether a row should be hidden. For example, create a function that returns FALSE if an address contains 'EU' or 'Europe', and TRUE otherwise.
practical_workflow.reason: The UDF defines the condition for hiding rows. It must be in Unity Catalog and you must have EXECUTE permission on it to use it in a policy.

practical_workflow.action: In the Databricks UI, navigate to Catalog > your catalog > Policies tab, then click 'New policy'.
practical_workflow.reason: This opens the policy creation form where you'll configure who the policy applies to and what condition it uses.

practical_workflow.action: Fill in the policy details: Name (e.g., 'hide_eu_customers'), Description, Applied to (e.g., 'All account users'), Scope (your catalog and schemas), and Purpose ('Hide table rows').
practical_workflow.reason: These settings define the scope and target of the policy—who it applies to and where.

practical_workflow.action: In Conditions, click 'Select existing', then 'Select function', and choose your UDF from the catalog and schema.
practical_workflow.reason: This tells the policy which function to use to decide whether to hide rows.

practical_workflow.action: In Function parameters, choose 'Map column to parameter if it has a specific tag', then search for and select the tag (e.g., 'pii : address').
practical_workflow.reason: This automatically passes the value of any column with that tag to the UDF. The UDF evaluates the column value and returns TRUE (hide row) or FALSE (show row).

practical_workflow.action: Optionally, expand 'Test function' and enter a sample value (e.g., an EU address) to verify the UDF returns the expected result before creating the policy.
practical_workflow.reason: Testing ensures your UDF logic is correct before the policy goes live.

practical_workflow.action: Click 'Create policy'. The policy is now active.
practical_workflow.reason: Once created, the policy automatically hides rows for all users in the 'Applied to' group based on the UDF condition.

practical_workflow.action: Run SELECT * FROM your_table to verify that only non-hidden rows are returned.
practical_workflow.reason: This confirms the policy is working—you should see only rows where the UDF returned FALSE (i.e., non-EU addresses in this example).

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking the UDF returns TRUE to show a row and FALSE to hide it.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: In this example, the UDF returns FALSE to hide a row (meaning 'it is an EU address, so hide it') and TRUE to show it (meaning 'it is not an EU address, so show it'). Always check your UDF logic—the meaning of TRUE/FALSE depends on what your function does.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Creating a policy without having MANAGE permission on the table or owning the table.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You must have MANAGE permission on the object or own it to create a policy on it. Check your permissions first.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to use a UDF in a policy when it's not in Unity Catalog or you don't have EXECUTE permission on it.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The UDF must be in Unity Catalog and you must have EXECUTE permission on it. Create the UDF in the correct catalog and ensure your permissions are set.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to tag columns before creating a policy that uses 'Map column to parameter if it has a specific tag'.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If you want the policy to automatically find columns by tag, you must tag them first using ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming the policy applies to all tables in the catalog automatically.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The policy applies only to the scope you specify (e.g., specific schemas or all schemas in a catalog). Check the Scope setting to confirm it covers the tables you want.

project_usage_notes: Use this pattern when you have sensitive data (like customer addresses or SSNs) and need to hide rows from certain users based on business rules. For example, hide EU customer records from non-EU teams due to GDPR compliance.
Tag columns consistently across your tables (e.g., all PII columns get 'pii' = 'column_type'). This lets you reuse the same policy across multiple tables without recreating it.
Test your UDF with realistic data before creating the policy. Use the 'Test function' feature to verify edge cases (e.g., 'E.U.' vs 'EU' vs 'Europe').
Remember that policies are applied at query time—when a user runs SELECT, the policy automatically filters rows. The user doesn't see hidden rows in the result set.
If you need to hide columns instead of rows, create a column mask policy instead. The workflow is similar but uses 'Hide columns' as the Purpose.
Policies are enforced for all users in the 'Applied to' group. If you need different rules for different groups, create separate policies with different conditions or UDFs.

reference_note.title: Creating and Applying Column Masking Policies with UDFs in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Learn how to create a User-Defined Function (UDF) that masks sensitive data like SSNs, then apply it as a column masking policy in Databricks Unity Catalog. Masking policies automatically hide sensitive column values from unauthorized users while keeping the data accessible to those with proper permissions. This is essential for protecting personally identifiable information (PII) in real projects.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A custom function you create in SQL that performs a specific operation. In this case, the mask_SSN function takes an SSN input and returns a masked version (***-**-****).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: UDFs let you define custom data transformation logic that can be reused across policies and queries. For masking, you need a UDF to define exactly how sensitive data should be hidden.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that automatically hides or transforms sensitive column values for certain users or groups. When a masked column is queried, the masking function runs automatically instead of returning the real value.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Masking policies enforce data security at the database level, so you don't have to manually filter sensitive data in every query. Different users see different data based on their permissions.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Labels you attach to columns to mark them as containing sensitive data. In this example, the 'pii : ssn' tag marks SSN columns as personally identifiable information.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tags let you apply policies to columns automatically based on their data type, rather than manually selecting each column. This scales better as your data grows.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Databricks' centralized metadata and governance system that manages catalogs, schemas, tables, and access control policies.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Policies must be created within Unity Catalog, and UDFs used in policies must be stored in Unity Catalog for security and auditability.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: MANAGE permission lets you create or modify policies on an object. EXECUTE permission lets you use a UDF in a policy.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You need the right permissions to create policies and use UDFs. In a real project, this prevents unauthorized users from bypassing security rules.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a User-Defined Function (UDF) in Databricks. The function takes input parameters and returns a result. In this example, it takes an SSN string and returns a masked version.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to define custom logic for data transformation, validation, or masking that will be reused across queries or policies.

important_parameters.meaning: The name you use to call the function later
Defines what data type the function accepts
The output the function produces

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog > Policies tab
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: The UI section in Databricks where you view and create column masking policies for a catalog.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to set up data masking rules for sensitive columns in your catalog.

important_features_or_tools.name: New policy
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a new masking policy that will automatically mask column values based on conditions you define.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to protect sensitive data from unauthorized users.

important_features_or_tools.name: Policy Name
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: The identifier for your policy (e.g., 'mask_ssn'). Used to reference the policy in logs and management.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Always required when creating a policy.

important_features_or_tools.name: Description
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A human-readable explanation of what the policy does and why it exists.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Always recommended for documentation and team clarity.

important_features_or_tools.name: Applied to...
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which principals (users, groups, or service principals) the masking policy applies to. In this example, 'All account users' means everyone sees masked data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to define who the policy affects. You can select specific groups or all users.

important_parameters.meaning: Users, groups, or service principals the policy applies to

important_features_or_tools.name: Except for...
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to exclude specific principals from the masking policy. Left blank means no exceptions.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When certain users (like data admins or compliance officers) should see unmasked data while others see masked data.

important_features_or_tools.name: Scope
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Defines which catalog and schemas the policy applies to. In this example, the 'abac' catalog and 'All schemas' within it.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to apply a policy to specific parts of your data warehouse rather than everything.

important_parameters.meaning: The catalog where the policy applies
Which schemas within the catalog are affected

important_features_or_tools.name: Purpose
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies the type of policy. 'Mask column data' means the policy will hide or transform column values.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When creating a masking policy (as opposed to other policy types).

important_parameters.meaning: The type of policy action

important_features_or_tools.name: Conditions > Mask column if it has specific tag
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Tells the policy to apply masking only to columns that have a specific tag. In this example, columns tagged with 'pii : ssn' will be masked.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to automatically mask all columns of a certain type without manually selecting each one.

important_parameters.meaning: The tag that identifies which columns to mask

important_features_or_tools.name: Select existing > Select function
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to choose which UDF will perform the masking. You navigate to the catalog, schema, and function name.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When setting up the masking policy to specify which function transforms the data.

important_parameters.meaning: Where the UDF is stored
The schema containing the UDF
The UDF name

important_features_or_tools.name: Test function
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to test the masking function before applying the policy. You provide sample input and see the masked output.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Before creating the policy, to verify the masking function works as expected.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking the UDF must be created inside the policy. Actually, you create the UDF first as a separate object, then reference it in the policy.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always create and test your UDF before creating the policy. The policy just tells Databricks when and how to use the UDF.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting that the UDF must be in Unity Catalog. If it's not, the policy won't be able to use it.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Make sure your UDF is created in a Unity Catalog schema (e.g., abac.customers.mask_ssn), not in a workspace-level schema.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming masking policies only hide data. They actually transform data using the UDF, so you can customize exactly what users see.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The UDF controls the output. You could mask with '***-**-****', or with a hash, or with a partial value like '***-**-5678'. It's flexible.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not understanding that masking is automatic. Once a policy is created, every query automatically applies the masking function without extra code.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Masking happens at the database layer, not in your query. Users don't need to do anything special; they just see masked data when they query.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing 'Applied to...' with 'Except for...'. Applied to defines who sees masked data; Except for defines who bypasses the mask.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If you set 'Applied to: All account users' and 'Except for: Data Admins', then everyone sees masked data except Data Admins, who see real values.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking tags are optional. If you use 'Mask column if it has specific tag', the column must actually have that tag or the policy won't apply.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Make sure columns are tagged with the correct tag (e.g., 'pii : ssn') before creating the policy, or the masking won't work.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, masking policies protect PII (personally identifiable information) like SSNs, credit card numbers, or email addresses. Once set up, they work automatically on every query, so you don't have to manually filter sensitive data in application code.
Use tags to organize which columns need masking. For example, tag all SSN columns with 'pii : ssn', all email columns with 'pii : email', etc. Then create one policy per tag type.
Test your masking function thoroughly before applying it to production data. Use the 'Test function' feature to verify the output looks correct.
Consider who should see unmasked data. Use 'Except for...' to allow data admins, compliance officers, or specific roles to see real values while regular users see masked data.
Masking policies work alongside row filters. In the example, SSNs are masked AND only non-EU residents are returned because both a masking policy and a row filter are active.
Remember that masking happens at query time, so there's no performance penalty for storing masked data. The real data is stored normally; masking just transforms what users see.
Document your masking policies with clear descriptions so team members understand why each policy exists and what data it protects.

This tutorial shows you how to configure row filter and column mask ABAC policies in Unity Catalog using SQL. For the Catalog Explorer UI-based version, see Tutorial: Configure ABAC.

In this example, an analytics team cannot access EU customer records, and SSNs are always masked. Customers who have consented to data sharing have their full email shown. Others see a masked version only.

This tutorial includes the following steps:

- Create governed tags
- Create a Unity Catalog catalog, schema, and table
- Apply governed tags to columns
- Create a UDF to detect EU addresses
- Create a row filter policy
- Test the row filter
- Create a UDF to mask SSNs
- Create a column mask policy
- Test the column mask

After completing these steps, you can optionally extend the tutorial with conditional email masking (steps 10–12).

- Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above, or serverless compute.
- Account admin or workspace admin permissions (to create governed tags).
- `MANAGE`permission on the target catalog or schema.
- `EXECUTE`on the UDFs.

Compute running older runtimes cannot access tables secured by ABAC.

Governed tags are key-value pairs defined at the account level. ABAC policies use them to discover which columns to filter or mask. In this tutorial, you create two governed tags:

- A `pii`tag with three allowed values:`ssn`,`address`, and`email`
- A `consent`key-only tag (no allowed values) to identify consent columns

To create a governed tag, you must have the governed tag CREATE permission at the account level. Account and workspace admins have CREATE by default.

- In your Databricks workspace, click  **Catalog**.
- Click the  **Govern**button.
- In the dropdown menu, click **Governed Tags**.
- Click **Create governed tag**.
- For the tag key, enter `pii`.
- Enter a description for the governed tag.
- For allowed values, enter: `ssn`,`address`, and`email`. Only these values can be assigned to this tag key.
- Click **Create**.
- Repeat steps 4–8 to create a second governed tag with the key `consent`. Leave the allowed values empty (key-only tag).

Tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally. Do not use tag names, values, or descriptors that could compromise the security of your resources. For example, do not use tag names, values or descriptors that contain personal or sensitive information.

Create a catalog, schema, and table with customer profiles. The `has_consent` column is used later for conditional email masking. Customers who have given consent (`TRUE`) have their full email shown.

Run the following commands in a notebook attached to compute on Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above:

CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS abac_tutorial;
USE CATALOG abac_tutorial;
-- Create schema
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS customers;
USE SCHEMA customers;

reference_note.title: Configure Row Filter and Column Mask ABAC Policies in Unity Catalog
reference_note.summary: Learn how to set up Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) in Databricks Unity Catalog using SQL to restrict row access and mask sensitive columns. This tutorial covers creating governed tags, building UDFs for filtering and masking logic, and applying row filter and column mask policies to protect sensitive data like SSNs and EU customer records based on user attributes and data consent.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A security approach that uses attributes (like user role or data properties) to decide who can see what data. Instead of giving blanket access, ABAC lets you hide specific rows or mask specific columns based on rules.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In real projects, you often need fine-grained control over sensitive data. ABAC lets you enforce policies automatically without manually managing access for each user.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Key-value pairs defined at the account level that label columns with metadata. They act as markers that ABAC policies use to identify which columns to filter or mask.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Governed tags are the foundation of ABAC. They tell Databricks which columns contain sensitive data (like PII) so policies know what to protect.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that hides entire rows from certain users based on conditions. For example, hiding all EU customer records from an analytics team.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Row filters prevent users from seeing data they shouldn't access at all, not just masking it. This is critical for compliance and data governance.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that hides or transforms sensitive values within a column while keeping the row visible. For example, showing 'XXX-XX-1234' instead of a full SSN.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Column masks let users see data they need while protecting sensitive details. This is useful when you want to share data but hide specific sensitive fields.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Custom SQL functions you write to implement the logic for filtering rows or masking values. For example, a UDF that detects if an address is in the EU.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: UDFs let you implement complex filtering and masking logic tailored to your business rules. They make policies flexible and reusable.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking governed tags are the same as regular tags. Governed tags are account-level metadata used by ABAC policies, not user-defined tags.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Governed tags are special tags created by admins at the account level. They are the mechanism that ABAC policies use to identify sensitive columns. Regular tags are different.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting that compute running older runtimes cannot access tables secured by ABAC.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always use Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above (or serverless compute) when working with ABAC-protected tables. Older runtimes will fail to access the data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Storing sensitive information (like personal data) in tag names, values, or descriptions.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Tag data is stored as plain text and may be replicated globally. Use generic tag names and values (like 'pii', 'ssn', 'address') instead of actual sensitive data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing row filters with column masks. Row filters hide entire rows; column masks hide values within columns.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Use row filters when you want to prevent users from seeing any data in certain rows (e.g., all EU customer records). Use column masks when you want users to see rows but hide specific sensitive values (e.g., masking SSNs).

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not testing ABAC policies before applying them to production data.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always test row filters and column masks with sample data first. Query the table as different users to verify that the correct rows are hidden and values are masked.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, you would create governed tags once at the account level, then reuse them across multiple catalogs and tables. This keeps your ABAC policies consistent.
Row filters are useful for compliance scenarios where certain teams cannot access data from specific regions or customers (e.g., analytics team cannot see EU customer records).
Column masks are useful for sharing data while protecting sensitive details. For example, you might share customer data with a partner but mask SSNs and full email addresses.

Conditional masking (using the 'has_consent' column) lets you apply different rules based on data properties. This is useful when data sharing rules depend on customer preferences or legal agreements.
Always ensure that users who need to access ABAC-protected tables have the correct permissions: EXECUTE on the UDFs and appropriate access to the catalog or schema.

Test ABAC policies thoroughly before rolling them out to production. Use sample data that includes edge cases (e.g., EU addresses with different formats) to verify that filtering and masking logic works correctly.

source_content:
Tag the `ssn_number`, `home_address`, and `email` columns with the `pii` governed tag. ABAC policies match columns by tag, not by name.

The `has_consent` column is tagged with the `consent` governed tag. This is required for the consent-aware masking policy in Step 11, which passes `has_consent` to the UDF via `USING COLUMNS`.

```
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.customers.profiles
ALTER COLUMN ssn_number
SET TAGS ('pii' = 'ssn');
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.customers.profiles
ALTER COLUMN home_address
SET TAGS ('pii' = 'address');
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.customers.profiles
ALTER COLUMN email
SET TAGS ('pii' = 'email');
ALTER TABLE abac_tutorial.customers.profiles
ALTER COLUMN has_consent
SET TAGS ('consent' = '');
```

This UDF is passed the value of every column tagged `pii = address` and returns:

- `FALSE`if the address contains- `EU`,- `E.U.`, or- `Europe`— the row is hidden.
- `TRUE`otherwise — the row is shown.

```
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION is_not_eu_address(address STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN (
    SELECT CASE
        WHEN LOWER(address) LIKE '%eu%'
          OR LOWER(address) LIKE '%e.u.%'
          OR LOWER(address) LIKE '%europe%'
        THEN FALSE
        ELSE TRUE
    END
);
```
This is a simplified check for demonstration purposes. In production, use a more robust method such as a country code column or a lookup table to determine region.

To create a policy, you must have `MANAGE` on the object or ownership of the object. To add a UDF to a policy, you must have `EXECUTE` on the UDF.

```
CREATE POLICY hide_eu_customers
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.customers
ROW FILTER is_not_eu_address
TO `account users`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('pii', 'address') AS addr_col
USING COLUMNS (addr_col);
```
You can also create policies through the Catalog Explorer UI. See Create and manage row filter and column mask policies for details.

Run the following query to verify that the row filter policy is working.

```
SELECT * FROM abac_tutorial.customers.profiles;
```
Only the 10 non-EU resident rows are returned. The five EU customers (Liam, Sophie, Hans, Elena, and Johan) are hidden.

This UDF returns a fully-redacted placeholder for any SSN value passed to it.

```
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION redact_ssn(ssn STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN '***-**-****';
```

Create a policy that targets all columns tagged `pii = ssn` and applies the `redact_ssn` function to each.

```
CREATE POLICY redact_ssn_policy
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.customers
COLUMN MASK redact_ssn
TO `account users`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('pii', 'ssn') AS ssn_col
ON COLUMN ssn_col;
```

Run the following query to verify that both the row filter and column mask are active.

```
SELECT * FROM abac_tutorial.customers.profiles;
```
SSNs now return as `***-**-****`. Only non-EU residents are returned because the row filter is also active.

The following steps extend the tutorial with consent-aware email masking. Customers who opted in (`has_consent = TRUE`) have their full email shown; others see only the first character and domain.

This UDF takes two arguments:

- `email`: the actual email value from the matched column
- `consent`: the value of the- `has_consent`column on the same row

```
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION mask_email_by_consent(email STRING, consent BOOLEAN)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN consent = TRUE THEN email
  ELSE CONCAT(LEFT(email, 1), '***@', SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1))
END;
```

reference_note.title: Tagging Columns and Creating Row Filter & Column Mask Policies in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Learn how to tag sensitive columns in Databricks tables, then use those tags to create row filter policies (hide entire rows) and column mask policies (redact sensitive data). Tags match columns by their metadata, not by name, which makes policies flexible and reusable. You'll also learn how to create consent-aware masking that shows different data based on user consent.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Labels you attach to columns that describe what kind of data they contain (e.g., 'pii' for personally identifiable information, 'consent' for consent flags). Tags are metadata, not part of the data itself.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Policies match columns by tag, not by column name. This means you can apply the same policy to any column with the same tag, even if columns have different names across tables.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that hides entire rows from certain users based on a condition. If the condition is FALSE, the row is hidden; if TRUE, the row is shown.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Use this when you need to prevent users from seeing entire records (e.g., hiding EU customer records from non-EU users).

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A rule that redacts or transforms the value of a column before showing it to a user. The actual data stays unchanged in the database; only what the user sees is masked.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Use this when you need to hide sensitive values within a row (e.g., showing '***-**-****' instead of a real SSN) while still letting users see the row.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Custom SQL functions that define the logic for filtering rows or masking columns. You write the logic once and reuse it across policies.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: UDFs let you implement complex business logic (e.g., checking if an address contains 'EU', or masking emails based on consent) without hardcoding rules into every policy.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A masking policy that shows different data to different users based on whether they have consent. For example, show full email to users who opted in, but mask it for others.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Allows you to respect user privacy preferences while still showing data to users who have given consent.

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Attaches a governed tag to a specific column in a table. The tag is a key-value pair (e.g., 'pii' = 'ssn').
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to label columns with metadata so policies can find and apply rules to them.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the tag (e.g., 'pii', 'consent')
The value assigned to the tag (e.g., 'ssn', 'address', 'email'). Can be empty string.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Defines a custom SQL function that can be used in policies. The function contains the logic for filtering or masking.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to implement custom business logic for row filtering or column masking.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the function (e.g., 'is_not_eu_address', 'redact_ssn')
The columns or values the function receives (e.g., address STRING, email STRING, consent BOOLEAN)
The data type the function returns (BOOLEAN for row filters, STRING for column masks)

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE POLICY ... ROW FILTER
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a row filter policy that hides entire rows based on a UDF condition. Applies to all tables in a schema that match the column tag criteria.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to prevent users from seeing entire records based on a condition.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the policy (e.g., 'hide_eu_customers')
The schema where the policy applies
The UDF that determines which rows to show (TRUE) or hide (FALSE)
The users or groups the policy applies to

important_parameters.parameter: MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value(tag_key, tag_value) AS alias
important_parameters.meaning: Finds all columns with a specific tag and assigns them an alias for use in the UDF
Specifies which columns to pass to the UDF

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE POLICY ... COLUMN MASK
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a column mask policy that redacts or transforms column values before showing them to users. The actual data in the database is unchanged.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to hide sensitive values within a row (e.g., SSNs, partial emails) while still showing the row.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the policy (e.g., 'redact_ssn_policy')
The UDF that transforms the column value
The alias of the column to mask (from MATCH COLUMNS)

important_parameters.parameter: MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value(tag_key, tag_value) AS alias
important_parameters.meaning: Finds all columns with a specific tag

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer UI
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A graphical interface in Databricks where you can create and manage row filter and column mask policies without writing SQL.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you prefer a visual interface over SQL commands, or when you want to manage policies through the Databricks UI.

important_features_or_tools.name: USING COLUMNS clause
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which columns to pass as arguments to the UDF in a policy. Used for consent-aware masking where you need to pass multiple columns (e.g., email and has_consent).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When your masking UDF needs access to multiple columns from the same row (e.g., the email column and a consent flag).

important_parameters.meaning: The aliases of columns to pass to the UDF, separated by commas

practical_workflow.action: Identify which columns contain sensitive data (e.g., SSN, email, address, consent flags).
practical_workflow.reason: You need to know what to tag before you can create policies.

practical_workflow.action: Use ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAGS to tag each sensitive column with a governed tag (e.g., 'pii' = 'ssn').
practical_workflow.reason: Tags are the mechanism policies use to find and apply rules to columns. Tagging by metadata (not name) makes policies reusable across tables.

practical_workflow.action: Create a UDF for each filtering or masking rule using CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION. For row filters, return BOOLEAN; for column masks, return STRING.
practical_workflow.reason: UDFs contain the business logic. Row filter UDFs return TRUE (show row) or FALSE (hide row). Column mask UDFs return the transformed value.

practical_workflow.action: Create a ROW FILTER policy using CREATE POLICY ... ROW FILTER. Use MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value() to find columns by tag, and pass them to the UDF via USING COLUMNS.
practical_workflow.reason: Row filter policies hide entire rows based on conditions. This prevents users from seeing records they shouldn't access.

practical_workflow.action: Create COLUMN MASK policies using CREATE POLICY ... COLUMN MASK for each sensitive column type. Use MATCH COLUMNS to find columns by tag.
practical_workflow.reason: Column mask policies redact sensitive values. Multiple masks can apply to the same table (e.g., one for SSN, one for email).

practical_workflow.action: For consent-aware masking, create a UDF that takes multiple arguments (e.g., email and consent flag). Use USING COLUMNS to pass both columns to the UDF.
practical_workflow.reason: Consent-aware masking shows different data based on user preferences. The UDF receives both the sensitive value and the consent flag to decide what to show.

practical_workflow.action: Test the policies by running SELECT queries on the table. Verify that rows are hidden (row filter) and values are masked (column mask) as expected.
practical_workflow.reason: Testing ensures policies work correctly before deploying to production.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking policies match columns by name instead of by tag.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Policies use tags (metadata) to find columns, not column names. This is why tagging is the first step. Two columns with different names but the same tag will both be affected by the same policy.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing row filters and column masks.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Row filters hide entire rows (return BOOLEAN: TRUE = show, FALSE = hide). Column masks redact values within a row (return the transformed value, usually STRING). Use row filters for access control, column masks for data redaction.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to tag the consent column when creating consent-aware masking policies.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If you want a UDF to receive the consent flag via USING COLUMNS, the consent column must be tagged (e.g., 'consent' = ''). The tag doesn't need a meaningful value, but it must exist.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Writing overly simplistic logic in UDFs (e.g., checking if address LIKE '%eu%').
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The tutorial notes that simple string matching is for demonstration only. In production, use robust methods like country code columns or lookup tables to determine region or other attributes.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not having the required permissions to create policies.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: To create a policy, you must have MANAGE permission on the schema or own the schema. To add a UDF to a policy, you must have EXECUTE permission on the UDF. Check your permissions before attempting to create policies.

project_usage_notes: Start by tagging all sensitive columns in your tables (PII, financial data, health data, etc.). This is a one-time setup that makes all future policies easier to manage.
Create reusable UDFs for common filtering and masking logic. For example, if multiple tables have SSNs, one redact_ssn UDF can be used in policies across all of them.
Use row filters for access control (e.g., hiding records based on geography, department, or data classification). Use column masks for data redaction (e.g., hiding SSNs, emails, or phone numbers).
For consent-aware masking, ensure the consent column is tagged and passed to the UDF via USING COLUMNS. This allows the UDF to make decisions based on user preferences.
Test policies thoroughly before deploying to production. Run SELECT queries as different users to verify that rows are hidden and values are masked correctly.
In production, replace simple string-matching logic in UDFs with robust methods (e.g., country code lookups, reference tables, or external APIs) to ensure accuracy.
Policies apply at query time, not at storage time. The actual data in the database is unchanged; only what users see is filtered or masked. This means you can audit the original data if needed.

source_content:
This policy targets columns tagged `pii = email` and passes the `has_consent` column to the UDF.

The `has_consent` column was tagged with the `consent` governed tag in Step 3. This is required because `USING COLUMNS` can only reference columns that are matched via `MATCH COLUMNS`. Even though `has_consent` is not being masked, it must be tagged so the policy can pass its value to the UDF.

```
CREATE POLICY mask_email_by_consent_policy
ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.customers
COLUMN MASK mask_email_by_consent
TO `account users`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('pii', 'email') AS email_col,
  has_tag('consent') AS consent_col
ON COLUMN email_col
USING COLUMNS (consent_col);
```

Run the following query to verify that all three policies are working together.

```
SELECT * FROM abac_tutorial.customers.profiles;
```
Customers with `has_consent = TRUE` have their full email shown. Customers with `has_consent = FALSE` see a masked version. SSNs remain fully masked, and only non-EU customers are returned.

| first_name | has_consent | ssn_number | |
|---|---|---|---|
| John | TRUE | ***-**-**** | |
| Jane | FALSE | j***@example.com | ***-**-**** |
| Alice | TRUE | ***-**-**** | |
| Bob | FALSE | b***@example.com | ***-**-**** |
| Charlie | TRUE | ***-**-**** | |
| Emily | FALSE | e***@example.com | ***-**-**** |
| Frank | TRUE | ***-**-**** | |
| Grace | TRUE | ***-**-**** | |
| Hank | FALSE | h***@example.com | ***-**-**** |
| Ivy | TRUE | ***-**-**** |

This tutorial demonstrated three ABAC patterns:

- **Row filtering**: hide rows based on column values matched by governed tags
- **Column masking**: mask columns matched by governed tags
- **Conditional masking**: mask a column based on another column's value on the same row, by tagging the context column and passing it to the UDF via- `USING COLUMNS`

To remove all objects created in this tutorial, run the following. If you skipped the conditional email masking steps, the `DROP POLICY mask_email_by_consent_policy` and `DROP FUNCTION mask_email_by_consent` statements fail, which is expected.

```
DROP POLICY hide_eu_customers ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.customers;
DROP POLICY redact_ssn_policy ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.customers;
DROP POLICY mask_email_by_consent_policy ON SCHEMA abac_tutorial.customers;
DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS abac_tutorial.customers.is_not_eu_address;
DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS abac_tutorial.customers.redact_ssn;
DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS abac_tutorial.customers.mask_email_by_consent;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS abac_tutorial.customers.profiles;
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS abac_tutorial.customers CASCADE;
```
To remove the `pii` and `consent` governed tags, use the Catalog Explorer UI.

reference_note.title: Conditional Column Masking with Governed Tags and UDFs in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Databricks allows you to create conditional masking policies that mask data based on values in other columns. You do this by tagging both the column to mask and the context column with governed tags, then passing the context column to a User Defined Function (UDF) via the USING COLUMNS clause. This enables fine-grained access control where the same column shows different values to different users based on their data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Labels you attach to columns that describe what kind of data they contain (like 'pii' for personally identifiable information or 'consent' for consent status). Policies use these tags to identify which columns to apply rules to.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Tags let you write policies once that automatically apply to any column with that tag, without hardcoding column names. This scales as your schema grows.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A clause in a policy that finds columns matching specific tag criteria. Only columns matched here can be referenced elsewhere in the policy.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: It's the mechanism that connects your policy to the actual columns in your table. Without matching columns, the policy has nothing to act on.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A clause that passes additional columns (beyond the one being masked) to a UDF so the UDF can make decisions based on their values.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Enables conditional logic: you can mask a column differently depending on the value of another column in the same row, like showing full email only if has_consent is TRUE.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Custom code you write that receives column values and returns a transformed value. In masking policies, the UDF receives the column to mask plus any context columns, and returns the masked result.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: UDFs let you implement custom masking logic beyond simple redaction, like conditional masking based on business rules.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A security approach where access decisions are based on attributes (tags and column values) rather than just user roles. Policies match attributes and apply rules accordingly.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: ABAC is more flexible and scalable than role-based access; you can enforce complex rules like 'mask email unless user has consent' without creating separate policies for each scenario.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE POLICY
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Creates a data masking or row filtering policy that automatically applies rules to query results based on matched columns and user context.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to enforce consistent data protection rules across a schema or table that apply to all queries.

important_parameters.meaning: Specifies which schema the policy applies to
Indicates this is a column masking policy (as opposed to row filtering)
Specifies which users or groups the policy applies to
Indicates the policy applies to tables (not views or other objects)
Defines which columns the policy targets using tag matching functions
important_parameters.example_value: has_tag_value('pii', 'email') AS email_col, has_tag('consent') AS consent_col

important_parameters.meaning: Specifies which matched column is the one being masked
Lists additional matched columns to pass to the UDF for conditional logic

important_features_or_tools.name: has_tag_value()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Matches columns that have a specific governed tag with a specific value. Returns the matched column with an alias.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to target columns with a specific tag and value combination, like all columns tagged 'pii' with value 'email'.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the governed tag to match
The specific value of the tag to match

important_features_or_tools.name: has_tag()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Matches columns that have a specific governed tag, regardless of the tag's value. Returns the matched column with an alias.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to target any column with a particular tag, like all columns tagged 'consent' regardless of their value.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the governed tag to match

important_features_or_tools.name: DROP POLICY
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Removes a masking or row filtering policy from a schema, stopping it from applying to future queries.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to remove or replace a policy, or clean up after testing.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the policy to drop
Specifies which schema the policy is in

important_features_or_tools.name: DROP FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Removes a user-defined function from the database.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When cleaning up UDFs used by policies, or when you no longer need custom masking logic.

important_parameters.meaning: Prevents an error if the function doesn't exist; useful when cleaning up optional components
The fully qualified name of the function to drop

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer UI
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks UI component for managing governed tags, viewing tag assignments, and managing metadata.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to create, edit, or remove governed tags; or when you want to see which columns have which tags.

practical_workflow.action: Tag your columns with governed tags using the Catalog Explorer UI. Tag the column to be masked (e.g., email) with a tag like 'pii' and value like 'email'. Tag any context columns (e.g., has_consent) with a tag like 'consent'.
practical_workflow.reason: Policies match columns by tags, not by name. Tagging makes columns discoverable by your policies and allows policies to scale as new columns are added.

practical_workflow.action: Create a UDF that implements your masking logic. The UDF should accept the column to mask plus any context columns, and return the masked value based on your business rules.
practical_workflow.reason: The UDF is where the actual conditional logic lives. It receives values from USING COLUMNS and decides what to return based on those values.

practical_workflow.action: Create a CREATE POLICY statement that: (a) uses MATCH COLUMNS with has_tag_value() and has_tag() to find the columns to mask and context columns, (b) specifies ON COLUMN to indicate which matched column gets masked, (c) uses USING COLUMNS to pass context columns to the UDF.
practical_workflow.reason: The policy ties together the tagged columns and the UDF. It tells Databricks which columns to mask, which UDF to use, and what additional data to pass to the UDF.

practical_workflow.action: Test the policy by running a SELECT query on the table. Verify that rows and columns are filtered/masked according to your rules.
practical_workflow.reason: Testing confirms the policy is working as intended before deploying to production.

practical_workflow.action: To clean up, use DROP POLICY to remove policies and DROP FUNCTION to remove UDFs. Use Catalog Explorer UI to remove governed tags.
practical_workflow.reason: Cleanup prevents unused policies and functions from cluttering your workspace and consuming resources.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to reference a column in USING COLUMNS that was not matched by MATCH COLUMNS.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Every column you want to use in a policy must be matched by MATCH COLUMNS first. Even if a column is not being masked, it must be tagged and matched so the policy can reference it.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that tagging a column is optional if you're not using it in the policy.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If you want to pass a column to a UDF via USING COLUMNS, it must be tagged and matched by MATCH COLUMNS, even if it's not the column being masked.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing has_tag() and has_tag_value().
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: has_tag() matches any column with a tag, regardless of value. has_tag_value() matches only columns with a specific tag and value. Use has_tag_value() when you need to target a specific subset of tagged columns.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming a policy applies to all users automatically.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The TO clause specifies which users or groups the policy applies to. If you specify TO `account users`, the policy only applies to those users; other users may see unmasked data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Writing complex masking logic directly in the policy instead of in a UDF.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Policies are declarative; they specify what to mask and which UDF to use. The actual masking logic belongs in the UDF, which is easier to test, version, and maintain.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, use conditional masking when you have columns that should be visible to some users but masked for others based on a condition. Example: show full email to users with consent, mask it for users without consent.
Always tag columns consistently across your schema. If you have multiple email columns, tag them all with 'pii' and 'email' so a single policy can protect all of them.
Test policies thoroughly before applying them to production tables. Use a test table with sample data to verify that masking works correctly for all combinations of conditions.

Document your UDFs and policies. Include comments explaining the business logic behind conditional masking rules so other team members understand why certain columns are masked under certain conditions.
Remember that policies apply at query time. The underlying data in the table is not modified; masking happens when users query the data. This means you can change policies without rewriting data.
Use DROP POLICY with IF EXISTS when writing cleanup scripts, especially if policies are optional or may not exist in all environments.

source_content:
Access control in Unity Catalog is built on the following complementary models:

- **Privileges and ownership**control- *who*can access- *what*, using grants on securable objects.
- **Attribute-based policies (ABAC)**control- *what*data users can access, using governed tags and centralized policies.
- **Table-level filtering and masking**control- *what*data users can see within tables using table-specific filters and views.
- **Workspace-level restrictions**control- *where*users can access data, by limiting objects to specific workspaces.

These models work together to enforce secure, fine-grained access across your data environment.

Workspace bindings, privileges, and ABAC policies all evaluate access at different levels, and they are designed to be used together. The following table compares them across common access control criteria:

Databricks recommends using attribute-based access control (ABAC) to centralize and scale access control based on governed tags. Use row filters and column masks only when you need per-table logic or haven't adopted ABAC yet.

| Mechanism | Applies to | Defined using | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catalogs, schemas, tables | Grants ( | Baseline access and delegation | |
| Tagged objects (tables, schemas) | Policies with governed tags and UDFs | Centralized, tag-driven policies and dynamic enforcement | |
| Individual tables | UDFs on the table itself | Table-specific filtering or masking | |
| Catalogs, external locations, storage credentials | Workspace assignment | Restricting access to objects from specific workspaces |

-
- Permissions concepts
- Understand the Unity Catalog object hierarchy, privilege inheritance, and how access flows from parent to child objects.

-
- Privileges reference
- View detailed descriptions of every privilege in Unity Catalog.

-
- Admin roles
- Learn about account admin, workspace admin, and metastore admin roles and their scopes.

-
- Manage privileges
- Grant, revoke, and inspect privileges on Unity Catalog objects using Catalog Explorer and SQL.

-
- Access requests
- Configure destinations for access requests on Unity Catalog securable objects, including email, Slack, Teams, and webhooks.

-
- Workspace-catalog binding
- Restrict which workspaces can access specific catalogs, external locations, and storage credentials.

-
- Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
- Define centralized, tag-driven policies that dynamically filter and mask data across your catalog.

-
- Row filters and column masks
- Apply per-table row and column filters using UDFs to control what data users see at query time.

reference_note.title: Access Control in Unity Catalog: Four Complementary Models
reference_note.summary: Databricks uses four complementary access control models to secure data: privileges and ownership (who accesses what), attribute-based policies or ABAC (what data users can access), table-level filtering and masking (what users see within tables), and workspace-level restrictions (where users can access data). These models work together to enforce fine-grained access. Databricks recommends using ABAC for centralized, scalable control based on governed tags, and using row filters and column masks only for table-specific logic or as a transitional approach.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Grants on securable objects determine who can access what. You assign permissions to users or groups on catalogs, schemas, tables, and other objects.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This is the baseline access control layer. You need to understand how to grant and revoke privileges to control who can see and use your data objects.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Uses governed tags and centralized policies to control what data users can access. Instead of managing individual permissions, you tag objects and create policies that apply to all tagged objects.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: ABAC scales better than manual privilege grants. As your data grows, managing access through tags and policies is more maintainable than granting individual permissions.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Row filters and column masks use user-defined functions (UDFs) to control what data users see within specific tables at query time.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Use this when you need fine-grained control within a single table, such as hiding sensitive columns or filtering rows based on user attributes.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Workspace bindings limit which workspaces can access specific catalogs, external locations, and storage credentials.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This controls where data can be accessed from. You can restrict sensitive data to specific workspaces, adding a geographic or organizational boundary to access.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Permissions flow from parent objects to child objects in the Unity Catalog hierarchy (catalog → schema → table).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Understanding inheritance helps you grant permissions efficiently at the right level without having to set permissions on every individual object.

important_features_or_tools.name: Grants
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Assigns privileges on securable objects (catalogs, schemas, tables, external locations, storage credentials) to users or groups.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to give users baseline access to data objects. This is the foundational access control mechanism.

important_features_or_tools.name: Governed Tags
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Tags applied to objects (tables, schemas) that are used by ABAC policies to dynamically control access.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When implementing ABAC. You tag objects with attributes (e.g., 'sensitivity=high', 'department=finance') and then create policies based on those tags.

important_features_or_tools.name: Attribute-Based Policies
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Centralized policies that use governed tags and UDFs to dynamically filter and mask data across your catalog.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Databricks recommends this as the primary access control mechanism for scaling access management. Use when you want tag-driven, centralized policies.

important_features_or_tools.name: Row Filters
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: UDFs applied to individual tables that filter which rows users can see at query time.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need table-specific row-level filtering or haven't yet adopted ABAC. Example: show only rows where department matches the user's department.

important_features_or_tools.name: Column Masks
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: UDFs applied to individual tables that mask (hide or redact) sensitive column values at query time.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need table-specific column-level masking or haven't yet adopted ABAC. Example: hide salary values for non-HR users.

important_features_or_tools.name: Workspace Bindings
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Restricts which workspaces can access specific catalogs, external locations, and storage credentials.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to enforce workspace-level access boundaries. Example: restrict a sensitive catalog to only the finance workspace.

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: UI tool for managing privileges on Unity Catalog objects.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you prefer a graphical interface to grant, revoke, and inspect privileges instead of using SQL.

important_features_or_tools.name: SQL Commands for Privilege Management
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: SQL statements to grant, revoke, and inspect privileges on Unity Catalog objects.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you prefer to manage privileges programmatically or in scripts. Alternative to using Catalog Explorer.

important_features_or_tools.name: Access Requests
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows users to request access to Unity Catalog securable objects. Requests can be routed to email, Slack, Teams, or webhooks.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to enable a self-service access request workflow. Users can request access instead of contacting admins directly.

important_parameters.meaning: Where access requests are sent

important_features_or_tools.name: Admin Roles
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Three types of admin roles with different scopes: account admin (entire account), workspace admin (single workspace), and metastore admin (metastore level).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When assigning administrative responsibilities. Understand the scope of each role to assign the right level of access.

important_parameters.meaning: Manages the entire Databricks account
Manages a single workspace
Manages the metastore level

practical_workflow.action: Understand your data hierarchy: organize data into catalogs, schemas, and tables in Unity Catalog.
practical_workflow.reason: Access control flows through this hierarchy. You need to know the structure before assigning permissions.

practical_workflow.action: Decide on your access control strategy: use ABAC (recommended) or a combination of privileges, row filters, and column masks.
practical_workflow.reason: Different strategies suit different needs. ABAC scales better for large organizations; row/column filters work for table-specific logic.

practical_workflow.action: If using ABAC: define governed tags for your objects (e.g., 'sensitivity=high', 'department=finance') and create centralized policies based on those tags.
practical_workflow.reason: ABAC is Databricks' recommended approach for scalable, centralized access control.

practical_workflow.action: If using privileges: grant permissions on catalogs, schemas, and tables to users or groups using Catalog Explorer or SQL GRANT commands.
practical_workflow.reason: Privileges provide baseline access control. Granting at the catalog or schema level is more efficient than granting on every table.

practical_workflow.action: If using row filters or column masks: define UDFs on specific tables to filter rows or mask columns at query time.
practical_workflow.reason: Use this for table-specific logic or as a transitional approach before adopting ABAC.

practical_workflow.action: If needed: set up workspace bindings to restrict which workspaces can access specific catalogs or external locations.
practical_workflow.reason: Workspace bindings add an organizational or geographic boundary to access control.

practical_workflow.action: Configure access requests so users can request access to objects instead of contacting admins directly.
practical_workflow.reason: This enables a self-service workflow and reduces admin overhead.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking you must choose between privileges, ABAC, and row/column filters.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: These models are complementary and work together. Use ABAC as your primary mechanism, and add row/column filters for table-specific logic. Privileges provide the baseline access layer.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Granting privileges on every individual table instead of using inheritance.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Grant privileges at the catalog or schema level when possible. Permissions flow down to child objects, so you don't need to grant on every table.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using row filters and column masks as the primary access control mechanism.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Databricks recommends using ABAC for centralized, scalable control. Use row/column filters only for table-specific logic or as a transitional approach.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not understanding the scope of admin roles.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Account admins manage the entire account, workspace admins manage a single workspace, and metastore admins manage the metastore level. Assign the right role for the right scope.

project_usage_notes: Start with ABAC and governed tags if you're building a new access control system. It scales better as your data and user base grow.
Use workspace bindings if your organization has multiple teams or departments that should not access each other's data.
Set up access requests early so users can request access without contacting admins. Route requests to Slack or email for visibility.
Document your tag strategy (what tags mean, which objects get tagged) so other admins can maintain it consistently.
Use Catalog Explorer to visually inspect and manage privileges. Use SQL commands for automation and scripting.
Test your access control policies with test users before rolling out to production. Verify that users see only the data they should.
If migrating from an older access control system, use row/column filters as a transitional approach while you implement ABAC.

source_content:
This page explains core concepts of the Unity Catalog permissions model, including the object model, privileges, ownership, and inheritance.

For a general reference of all Unity Catalog privileges, see Unity Catalog privileges reference. For instructions on granting and revoking privileges, see Show, grant, and revoke privileges.

In Unity Catalog, data and metadata live in a top-level container called a metastore. Within this metastore, data is represented as objects in a three-level namespace: `catalog`.`schema`.`table`. This hierarchical structure also provides the foundation for access control in Unity Catalog.

Every object in this hierarchy is a **securable object**. Access control in Unity Catalog works by granting privileges, such as `SELECT`, `MODIFY`, or `USE SCHEMA`, on these securable objects. This model provides fine-grained control over who can access and manage data across your organization.

For a complete list of securable objects and the privileges that apply to each, see Unity Catalog privileges reference.

Some securable objects in Unity Catalog are **container objects**, meaning they contain child objects within the hierarchy. Container objects have a special role in the permissions model because privileges granted on them can affect their children through inheritance.

The following are container objects in Unity Catalog:

- Catalogs: The top level of the three-level namespace. Catalogs contain schemas as direct children.
- Schemas: The middle level of the three-level namespace. Schemas contain tables, views, volumes, and functions as direct children.

Container objects have several important characteristics:

| Characteristic | Description |
|---|---|
| Privilege inheritance | When you grant a privilege on a container object, that privilege automatically applies to all current and future child objects. For example, granting  |
| Usage privileges | Access to child objects requires the appropriate  |
| Ability to manage child objects | When you own a container object, you automatically get the ability to manage all child objects, even if you don't own those children directly. See Ownership. |
| Creation privileges | Container objects support privileges that allow users to create child objects within them, such as  |

Non-container objects, like tables, views, volumes, and functions, don't contain child objects.

Privileges determine what actions a user or group can perform on a securable object. Common privileges include:

- `SELECT`: Read data from tables or views
- `MODIFY`: Write data to tables or views
- `USE CATALOG`: Access a catalog (requires additional privileges to work with child objects)
- `USE SCHEMA`: Access a schema (requires additional privileges to work with child objects)
- `CREATE TABLE`: Create tables within a schema

A user or group must be explicitly granted a privilege to perform an action.

The following sections describe important special privileges in Databricks. For a complete reference of all privileges, see Unity Catalog privileges reference.

reference_note.title: Unity Catalog Permissions Model: Objects, Privileges, and Access Control
reference_note.summary: Unity Catalog organizes data in a three-level hierarchy (catalog.schema.table) where every object is securable and access is controlled by granting specific privileges. Container objects (catalogs and schemas) pass privileges down to their children automatically, while non-container objects (tables, views, volumes, functions) stand alone. Users must be explicitly granted privileges like SELECT, MODIFY, or USE SCHEMA to perform actions.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Any object in Unity Catalog that can have access permissions applied to it. This includes catalogs, schemas, tables, views, volumes, and functions.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Understanding what is securable helps you know where you can apply permissions in your data organization. Every object you work with in Databricks needs explicit permission grants.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Data is organized as catalog.schema.table. Catalogs are the top level, schemas are the middle level, and tables/views/volumes/functions are at the bottom.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This hierarchy is the foundation for both organizing your data and controlling who can access it. You need to understand this structure to grant permissions correctly.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Objects that hold other objects inside them. In Unity Catalog, catalogs and schemas are container objects because they contain child objects.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Container objects have special behavior: privileges granted on them automatically apply to all current and future child objects. This saves time when setting up permissions for large groups of data.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When you grant a privilege on a container object (like a catalog or schema), that privilege automatically applies to all child objects within it, both now and in the future.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You don't have to grant permissions individually on every table. Granting at the container level is more efficient and ensures new objects get the right permissions automatically.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A user or group must be explicitly given permission to perform an action. Permissions are not automatic; they must be granted by someone with authority.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: This is a security principle. By default, no one can access data unless you explicitly grant them permission. This prevents accidental data exposure.

important_features_or_tools.name: Metastore
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A top-level container in Unity Catalog that holds all your data and metadata. It is the foundation of the entire permissions model.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Every Databricks workspace uses a metastore. You don't create it directly, but you need to understand it exists as the root of your data hierarchy.

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: The top level of the three-level namespace. Catalogs contain schemas as direct children and are container objects.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When organizing data into logical groups (e.g., one catalog for production data, one for analytics). Use catalogs to grant permissions to large groups of related data.

important_features_or_tools.name: Schema
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: The middle level of the three-level namespace. Schemas contain tables, views, volumes, and functions as direct children and are container objects.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When organizing related tables and objects within a catalog. Use schemas to group objects by team, project, or purpose.

important_features_or_tools.name: SELECT Privilege
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows a user or group to read data from tables or views.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want someone to view or query data but not modify it. This is the most common read permission.

important_features_or_tools.name: MODIFY Privilege
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows a user or group to write data to tables or views (insert, update, delete operations).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want someone to change data in a table. This is more powerful than SELECT and should be granted carefully.

important_features_or_tools.name: USE CATALOG Privilege
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows a user or group to access a catalog. However, additional privileges are required to actually work with child objects inside the catalog.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want someone to see a catalog exists, but they still need other privileges (like USE SCHEMA or SELECT) to do anything with the data inside.

important_features_or_tools.name: USE SCHEMA Privilege
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows a user or group to access a schema. However, additional privileges are required to actually work with objects inside the schema.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want someone to see a schema exists, but they still need other privileges (like SELECT or CREATE TABLE) to do anything with the objects inside.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE TABLE Privilege
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows a user or group to create new tables within a schema.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to let someone build new tables in a schema without giving them full control over existing tables.

practical_workflow.action: Understand your data hierarchy: identify which catalogs, schemas, and tables you need to control access to.
practical_workflow.reason: You need to know what objects exist before you can grant permissions on them. The hierarchy determines how permissions will flow.

practical_workflow.action: Identify who needs access (users or groups) and what they need to do (read, write, create, etc.).
practical_workflow.reason: This determines which privileges you need to grant. Different roles need different permissions.

practical_workflow.action: Decide whether to grant privileges at the container level (catalog or schema) or at the object level (table, view, etc.).
practical_workflow.reason: Granting at the container level is more efficient if many users need access to many objects, because privileges inherit to children automatically.
