If you must use custom data sources or JDBC drivers not in Lakehouse Federation, ensure users have SELECT privileges on ANY FILE at minimum, and MODIFY only if they need write access.
Store all new data in Unity Catalog volumes or tables. Reserve ANY FILE access for legacy data and temporary external integrations only.
Document which users/service principals have ANY FILE privileges and why, especially MODIFY privileges, as they represent a security boundary.

source_content:
This article describes the privilege model for the legacy Databricks Hive metastore, which is built in to each Databricks workspace. It also describes how to grant, deny, and revoke privileges for objects in the built-in Hive metastore. Unity Catalog uses a different model for granting privileges. See Unity Catalog privileges reference.

Table access control for data managed by the Hive metastore is a legacy data governance model. Databricks recommends that you upgrade the tables managed by the Hive metastore to the Unity Catalog metastore. Unity Catalog simplifies security and governance of your data by providing a central place to administer and audit data access across multiple workspaces in your account. To learn more about how the legacy privilege model differs from the Unity Catalog privilege model, see Work with the legacy Hive metastore alongside Unity Catalog.

- An administrator must enable and enforce table access control for the workspace.
- The cluster must be enabled for table access control.

- Data access control is *always enabled*in Databricks SQL even if table access control is*not enabled*for the workspace.
- If table access control is enabled for the workspace and you have already specified ACLs (granted and denied privileges) in the workspace, those ACLs are respected in Databricks SQL.

Privileges on data objects managed by the Hive metastore can be granted by either a workspace admin or the owner of an object. You can manage privileges for Hive metastore objects by using SQL commands.

To manage privileges in SQL, you use GRANT, REVOKE, DENY, MSCK, and SHOW GRANTS statements in a notebook or the Databricks SQL query editor, using the syntax:

```
GRANT privilege_type ON securable_object TO principal
```
Where:

- `privilege_type`is a Hive metastore privilege type
- `securable_object`is a securable object in the Hive metastore
- `principal`is a user, service principal (represented by its applicationId value), or group. You must enclose users, service principals, and group names with special characters in backticks (- `` ``). See Principal.

To grant a privilege to all users in your workspace, grant the privilege to the `users` group. For example:

```
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE <schema-name>.<table-name> TO users
```
For more information about managing privileges for objects in the Hive metastore using SQL commands, see Privileges and securable objects in the Hive metastore.

You can also manage table access control in a fully automated setup using the Databricks Terraform provider and databricks_sql_permissions.

When table access control is enabled on a cluster or SQL warehouse, a user who creates a schema, table, view, or function becomes its owner. The owner is granted all privileges and can grant privileges to other users.

Groups may own objects, in which case all members of that group are considered owners.

Either the owner of an object or a workspace admin can transfer ownership of an object using the following command:

```
ALTER <object> OWNER TO `<user-name>@<user-domain>.com`
```
When table access control is disabled on a cluster or SQL warehouse, owners are not registered when a schema, table, or view is created. A workspace admin must assign an owner to the object using the `ALTER <object> OWNER TO` command.

reference_note.title: Hive Metastore Privilege Model and Table Access Control
reference_note.summary: Databricks Hive metastore uses a legacy privilege model to control who can access tables, schemas, views, and functions. Workspace admins and object owners can grant, deny, or revoke privileges using SQL commands like GRANT and REVOKE. However, Databricks recommends upgrading to Unity Catalog for simpler, centralized security across multiple workspaces.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A built-in metadata storage system in each Databricks workspace that tracks tables, schemas, views, and functions. It is the legacy approach to organizing and securing data.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Understanding whether your workspace uses Hive metastore or Unity Catalog determines how you manage data access and security in your project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A system that controls who can read, write, or modify tables and other data objects. It must be enabled by a workspace admin and on individual clusters to work.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Without TAC enabled, anyone with cluster access can see all data. Enabling it lets you restrict data access to specific users or groups.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Permissions that grant specific actions on data objects. Examples include SELECT (read), MODIFY (write), and OWNER (full control).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Privileges let you control exactly what each user can do with each table or schema in your project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A user, service principal, or group that can be granted privileges. Service principals are identified by their applicationId value.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You need to identify who (or what application) should have access to your data before you can grant privileges.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: The user or group that created a schema, table, view, or function. The owner automatically gets all privileges and can grant privileges to others.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Ownership determines who controls access to data objects. If you create a table, you own it and can decide who else can use it.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A newer, centralized privilege model that replaces the legacy Hive metastore approach. It works across multiple workspaces in your account.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Databricks recommends upgrading to Unity Catalog for better security, simpler management, and audit capabilities across your entire organization.

important_features_or_tools.name: GRANT statement
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Gives a user, service principal, or group permission to perform a specific action on a data object.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to allow someone to access or modify a table, schema, view, or function.

important_parameters.meaning: The type of permission being granted (e.g., SELECT, MODIFY, OWNER)
The data object being protected (e.g., TABLE, SCHEMA, VIEW, FUNCTION)
The user, service principal, or group receiving the privilege

important_features_or_tools.name: REVOKE statement
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Removes a previously granted privilege from a user, service principal, or group.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to remove access that was previously granted.

important_parameters.meaning: The type of permission being removed
The data object from which access is being removed
The user, service principal, or group losing the privilege

important_features_or_tools.name: DENY statement
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Explicitly blocks a user, service principal, or group from performing an action, even if they have been granted that privilege elsewhere.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to prevent specific access that might otherwise be allowed through group membership or other grants.

important_parameters.meaning: The type of permission being denied
The data object being protected
The user, service principal, or group being denied access

important_features_or_tools.name: SHOW GRANTS statement
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Displays all privileges that have been granted or denied for a specific object or principal.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to audit or verify what access has been set up for a table, schema, or user.

important_features_or_tools.name: ALTER <object> OWNER TO statement
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Changes the owner of a schema, table, view, or function to a different user or group.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to transfer ownership of a data object, or when TAC is disabled and you need to assign an owner.

important_parameters.meaning: The data object whose owner is being changed (SCHEMA, TABLE, VIEW, or FUNCTION)
The new owner's email address, enclosed in backticks if it contains special characters

important_features_or_tools.name: MSCK statement
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Hive metastore command for managing metadata (mentioned as part of privilege management tools).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When managing Hive metastore metadata alongside privilege management.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks SQL Query Editor
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A web-based interface where you can write and execute SQL commands to manage privileges.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to grant, revoke, or audit privileges without writing code in a notebook.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks Notebooks
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: An interactive environment where you can write SQL commands to manage privileges alongside other code.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to manage privileges as part of a larger data pipeline or automation script.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks Terraform Provider (databricks_sql_permissions)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Allows you to automate privilege management using infrastructure-as-code, defining who has access to what in configuration files.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to manage privileges in a fully automated, version-controlled way as part of your infrastructure setup.

important_features_or_tools.name: users group
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A built-in group that represents all users in your workspace. Granting a privilege to 'users' gives that privilege to everyone.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to give all workspace users access to a table or schema.

important_features_or_tools.name: Databricks SQL
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A SQL query engine where data access control is always enabled, even if table access control is not enabled for the workspace.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When running SQL queries; note that access restrictions apply here regardless of workspace-level TAC settings.

practical_workflow.action: Check if your workspace uses Hive metastore or Unity Catalog. If using Hive metastore, confirm that table access control is enabled by a workspace admin.
practical_workflow.reason: You can only manage privileges if TAC is enabled. If it is not, you need to ask your admin to enable it first.

practical_workflow.action: Verify that the cluster or SQL warehouse you are using has table access control enabled.
practical_workflow.reason: TAC must be enabled on both the workspace level and the cluster/warehouse level for privilege management to work.

practical_workflow.action: Identify who needs access to your data: individual users, groups, or service principals.
practical_workflow.reason: You need to know the principals (users, groups, or service principals) before you can grant them privileges.

practical_workflow.action: Open the Databricks SQL query editor or a notebook and write a GRANT statement to give the appropriate privilege to each principal.
practical_workflow.reason: This is how you actually set up access control in the Hive metastore.

practical_workflow.action: Use SHOW GRANTS to verify that privileges were set up correctly.
practical_workflow.reason: Auditing ensures that the right people have the right access before your project goes live.

practical_workflow.action: If you need to remove or change access later, use REVOKE or DENY statements.
practical_workflow.reason: Access control is ongoing; you may need to adjust permissions as your project evolves.

practical_workflow.action: Consider upgrading to Unity Catalog if you manage multiple workspaces or need centralized governance.
practical_workflow.reason: Unity Catalog is the recommended modern approach and simplifies security across your organization.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming that table access control is enabled by default.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: TAC is not enabled by default. A workspace admin must explicitly enable it on the workspace and on each cluster or SQL warehouse. Without it, all users with cluster access can see all data.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that disabling TAC on a cluster removes all access control.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Data access control is always enabled in Databricks SQL, even if TAC is disabled on the cluster. Access restrictions still apply in SQL queries.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to enclose user names or service principal IDs with special characters in backticks.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If a principal's name contains special characters (like an email address with @), you must wrap it in backticks: `user@domain.com`.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing GRANT and DENY.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: GRANT gives permission; DENY blocks permission. DENY takes precedence, so if a user is both granted and denied a privilege, they are denied.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Not realizing that the object owner automatically has all privileges.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: When you create a table or schema with TAC enabled, you become the owner and automatically have full control. You do not need to grant yourself privileges.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking the Hive metastore privilege model is the same as Unity Catalog.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: They are different models. Hive metastore is legacy; Unity Catalog is the recommended modern approach. They have different privilege syntax and management approaches.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, you will likely create tables in a schema and then use GRANT statements to give specific teams or users SELECT access. For example: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE analytics.customer_data TO `analytics_team@company.com`.
If you have a service principal that runs automated jobs, you will need to grant it privileges using its applicationId value instead of an email address.
Use the users group to quickly give all workspace members access to shared reference tables: GRANT SELECT ON TABLE shared.reference_table TO users.
Audit access regularly using SHOW GRANTS to ensure that only the right people have access to sensitive data.
If your organization manages multiple workspaces, plan to migrate from Hive metastore to Unity Catalog so you can manage access centrally instead of per-workspace.

When table access control is disabled on a cluster, owners are not automatically assigned. A workspace admin must manually assign ownership using ALTER <object> OWNER TO, so plan for this if you are setting up a new cluster.

You can automate privilege management using the Databricks Terraform provider (databricks_sql_permissions) if you want to define access control as code and version-control it alongside your infrastructure.

source_content:
The securable objects are:

-
`CATALOG`: controls access to the entire data catalog.- `SCHEMA`: controls access to a schema.- `TABLE`: controls access to a managed or external table.
- `VIEW`: controls access to SQL views.
- `FUNCTION`: controls access to a named function.

-
`ANONYMOUS FUNCTION`: controls access to anonymous or temporary functions.note`ANONYMOUS FUNCTION`objects are not supported in Databricks SQL.
-
`ANY FILE`: controls access to the underlying filesystem.warningUsers granted access to `ANY FILE`can bypass the restrictions put on the catalog, schemas, tables, and views by reading from the filesystem directly.

Privileges on global and local temporary views are not supported. Local temporary views are visible only within the same session, and views created in the `global_temp` schema are visible to all users sharing a cluster or SQL warehouse. However, privileges on the underlying tables and views referenced by any temporary views are enforced.

- `SELECT`: gives read access to an object.
- `CREATE`: gives ability to create an object (for example, a table in a schema).
- `MODIFY`: gives ability to add, delete, and modify data to or from an object.
- `USAGE`: does not give any abilities, but is an additional requirement to perform any action on a schema object.
- `READ_METADATA`: gives ability to view an object and its metadata.
- `CREATE_NAMED_FUNCTION`: gives ability to create a named UDF in an existing catalog or schema.
- `MODIFY_CLASSPATH`: gives ability to add files to the Spark class path.
- `ALL PRIVILEGES`: gives all privileges (is translated into all the above privileges).

The `MODIFY_CLASSPATH` privilege is not supported in Databricks SQL.

`USAGE` privilege

To perform an action on a schema object in the Hive metastore, a user must have the `USAGE` privilege on that schema in addition to the privilege to perform that action. Any one of the following satisfies the `USAGE` requirement:

- Be a workspace admin
- Have the `USAGE`privilege on the schema or be in a group that has the`USAGE`privilege on the schema
- Have the `USAGE`privilege on the`CATALOG`or be in a group that has the`USAGE`privilege
- Be the owner of the schema or be in a group that owns the schema

Even the owner of an object inside a schema must have the `USAGE` privilege in order to use it.

When table access control is enabled on the workspace and on all clusters, SQL objects in Databricks are hierarchical and privileges are inherited downward. This means that granting or denying a privilege on the `CATALOG` automatically grants or denies the privilege to all schemas in the catalog. Similarly, privileges granted on a schema object are inherited by all objects in that schema. This pattern is true for all securable objects.

If you deny a user privileges on a table, the user can't see the table by attempting to list all tables in the schema. If you deny a user privileges on a schema, the user can't see that the schema exists by attempting to list all schemas in the catalog.

reference_note.title: Databricks Access Control: Securable Objects and Privileges
reference_note.summary: Databricks uses a hierarchical permission system to control who can access data. You grant or deny specific privileges (like SELECT, CREATE, MODIFY) on securable objects (CATALOG, SCHEMA, TABLE, VIEW, FUNCTION). Privileges flow downward—granting access to a CATALOG automatically grants it to all schemas and tables inside. Understanding this hierarchy is essential for setting up secure data access in any Databricks project.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: These are the things you can control access to in Databricks: CATALOG (entire data catalog), SCHEMA (a collection of tables), TABLE (managed or external), VIEW (SQL views), FUNCTION (named functions), ANONYMOUS FUNCTION (temporary functions), and ANY FILE (underlying filesystem).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When you set up a Databricks project, you need to know what level to grant permissions at. Granting at the CATALOG level is broader than granting at individual TABLE level.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Privileges are specific permissions you grant to users. Examples: SELECT (read), CREATE (make new objects), MODIFY (change data), USAGE (required to access schema objects), READ_METADATA (view object details), ALL PRIVILEGES (everything).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You grant the minimum privilege needed for each user's role. A data analyst might get SELECT; a data engineer might get CREATE and MODIFY.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When table access control is enabled, privileges granted at a higher level (like CATALOG) automatically apply to all lower levels (SCHEMA, TABLE, VIEW). If you grant SELECT on a CATALOG, all users get SELECT on all tables in it.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You can manage permissions efficiently by setting them at the right level instead of configuring each table individually. But you must understand the hierarchy to avoid accidentally granting too much access.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: USAGE is a special privilege that doesn't grant any ability by itself, but is required to perform ANY action on a schema object. Even the owner of a table must have USAGE on the schema to use it.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When setting up access, you must grant both USAGE on the schema AND the specific privilege (SELECT, CREATE, etc.) on the object. Missing USAGE will block access even if other privileges are granted.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: ANY FILE is a securable object that controls access to the underlying filesystem. Users with ANY FILE privilege can read directly from the filesystem and bypass all CATALOG, SCHEMA, TABLE, and VIEW restrictions.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Be very careful granting ANY FILE privilege. It can be used to circumvent your data governance. Only grant it to trusted users who need direct filesystem access.

important_features_or_tools.name: CATALOG
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Represents the entire data catalog. Granting or denying privileges on a CATALOG automatically applies to all schemas and objects inside it.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use CATALOG-level permissions when you want to give a user or group broad access to all data, or deny them access to everything.

important_features_or_tools.name: SCHEMA
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Represents a collection of tables and views. Privileges on a schema are inherited by all objects in that schema.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use SCHEMA-level permissions to control access to a logical grouping of related tables (e.g., all tables for a specific department or project).

important_features_or_tools.name: TABLE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Represents a managed or external table. You can grant or deny privileges on individual tables.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use TABLE-level permissions for fine-grained control when different users need access to different tables within the same schema.

important_features_or_tools.name: VIEW
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Represents a SQL view. You can control access to views separately from the underlying tables.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use VIEW-level permissions to give users access to filtered or aggregated data without exposing the full underlying table.

important_features_or_tools.name: FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Represents a named user-defined function (UDF). You can control who can use or create functions.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use FUNCTION-level permissions when you have shared UDFs that only certain users should be able to call or modify.

important_features_or_tools.name: ANONYMOUS FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Represents temporary or anonymous functions. Access control for these is available in some contexts but not in Databricks SQL.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Note: ANONYMOUS FUNCTION objects are not supported in Databricks SQL, so you typically won't use this in SQL-based projects.

important_features_or_tools.name: ANY FILE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Controls access to the underlying filesystem. Users with ANY FILE privilege can read directly from the filesystem and bypass catalog/schema/table restrictions.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant ANY FILE only to trusted users who need direct filesystem access. Be cautious—it can circumvent your data governance.

important_features_or_tools.name: SELECT
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Gives read access to an object (table, view, etc.).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant SELECT to users who need to query data but not modify it (e.g., data analysts, business users).

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Gives ability to create new objects (e.g., a table in a schema).
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant CREATE to data engineers or users who need to build new tables, schemas, or other objects.

important_features_or_tools.name: MODIFY
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Gives ability to add, delete, and modify data in an object.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant MODIFY to users who need to insert, update, or delete data (e.g., data engineers, ETL processes).

important_features_or_tools.name: USAGE
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Does not grant any ability by itself, but is required to perform any action on a schema object. Must be granted on the schema to use any object within it.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Always grant USAGE on a schema when you grant any other privilege on objects in that schema. Even object owners need USAGE on the schema.

important_features_or_tools.name: READ_METADATA
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Gives ability to view an object and its metadata (column names, data types, etc.) without being able to read the data.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant READ_METADATA to users who need to understand the structure of data but not access the actual values.

important_features_or_tools.name: CREATE_NAMED_FUNCTION
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Gives ability to create a named UDF in an existing catalog or schema.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant CREATE_NAMED_FUNCTION to data engineers or advanced users who need to create reusable functions.

important_features_or_tools.name: MODIFY_CLASSPATH
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Gives ability to add files to the Spark class path.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant MODIFY_CLASSPATH only to advanced users who need to add custom libraries. Note: Not supported in Databricks SQL.

important_features_or_tools.name: ALL PRIVILEGES
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Grants all privileges (SELECT, CREATE, MODIFY, USAGE, READ_METADATA, CREATE_NAMED_FUNCTION, MODIFY_CLASSPATH) at once.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Grant ALL PRIVILEGES to workspace admins or trusted power users who need full control.

practical_workflow.action: Identify the level at which you want to grant access: CATALOG (broadest), SCHEMA (medium), or TABLE/VIEW (most specific).
practical_workflow.reason: Privileges inherit downward, so choosing the right level makes permission management efficient and prevents accidental over-sharing.

practical_workflow.action: Determine what privilege each user or group needs: SELECT (read-only), CREATE (build objects), MODIFY (change data), READ_METADATA (see structure), or ALL PRIVILEGES (full control).
practical_workflow.reason: Granting the minimum necessary privilege follows security best practices and prevents accidental data modification.

practical_workflow.action: If granting access to objects in a schema, always grant USAGE on the schema first, then grant the specific privilege on the object.
practical_workflow.reason: USAGE is required to perform any action on schema objects. Without it, even SELECT won't work.

practical_workflow.action: Test access by logging in as the user and attempting to perform the intended action (e.g., SELECT from a table).
practical_workflow.reason: Verifies that your permission configuration is correct and the user can actually do what they need to do.

practical_workflow.action: Avoid granting ANY FILE privilege unless absolutely necessary. If you must grant it, restrict it to specific trusted users.
practical_workflow.reason: ANY FILE allows users to bypass all catalog/schema/table restrictions by reading directly from the filesystem, which can compromise data governance.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Granting a privilege on a table without granting USAGE on the schema. For example, granting SELECT on a table but not USAGE on the schema.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always grant USAGE on the schema in addition to the specific privilege. USAGE is a prerequisite for any action on schema objects.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that granting SELECT on a CATALOG means users can see all tables. They can see the tables, but if you deny SELECT on a specific TABLE, they won't see that table in listings.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Privileges are hierarchical and inherited downward, but denials also work downward. If you deny a privilege at any level, users can't see that object in listings.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Granting ANY FILE privilege thinking it's just for file-based operations. It actually allows users to bypass all data governance by reading directly from the filesystem.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: ANY FILE is a security risk. Only grant it to users who absolutely need direct filesystem access, and understand that they can circumvent your catalog/schema/table restrictions.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to set privileges on temporary views (local temporary views or views in `global_temp` schema).
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Privileges on temporary views are not supported. Instead, privileges on the underlying tables and views referenced by temporary views are enforced.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming that being the owner of an object means you can automatically use it.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Even the owner of an object must have USAGE privilege on the schema to use it. Ownership does not bypass the USAGE requirement.

project_usage_notes: When starting a Databricks project, plan your permission structure early. Decide which users need SELECT (analysts), CREATE (engineers), MODIFY (data pipelines), and READ_METADATA (data discovery). Use SCHEMA-level permissions for logical groupings to reduce management overhead.
Always grant USAGE on the schema before granting any other privilege on objects in that schema. This is a common setup step that's easy to forget but critical for access to work.
If you have sensitive tables, use TABLE-level permissions to restrict access. For example, grant SELECT on most tables but deny SELECT on a sensitive table, even if the user has SELECT on the schema.
Use READ_METADATA for users who need to understand data structure (column names, types) for documentation or data discovery tools, but don't need to see actual data values.
Avoid granting ANY FILE unless you have a specific use case. If you must grant it, audit which users have it and why, as it can be used to bypass your data governance.
Test your permission setup by logging in as different users and attempting to perform their expected tasks. This catches configuration errors before they affect real work.

Remember that privileges are inherited downward when table access control is enabled. Granting SELECT on a CATALOG automatically grants SELECT on all schemas and tables. Use this to simplify management, but be aware of the scope.

source_content:
Databricks includes two user functions that allow you to express column- and row-level permissions dynamically in the body of a view definition that is managed by the Hive metastore.

- `current_user()`: return the current user name.
- `is_member()`: determine if the current user is a member of a specific Databricks group at the workspace level.

The following example combines both functions to determine if a user has the appropriate group membership:

```
-- Return: true if the user is a member and false if they are not
SELECT
  current_user as user,
-- Check to see if the current user is a member of the "Managers" group.
  is_member("Managers") as admin
```

You can use dynamic views to limit the columns a specific group or user can see. Consider the following example where only users who belong to the `auditors` group are able to see email addresses from the `sales_raw` table. At analysis time Spark replaces the `CASE` statement with either the literal `'REDACTED'` or the column `email`. This behavior allows for all the usual performance optimizations provided by Spark.

```
-- Alias the field 'email' to itself (as 'email') to prevent the
-- permission logic from showing up directly in the column name results.
CREATE VIEW sales_redacted AS
SELECT
  user_id,
  CASE WHEN
    is_group_member('auditors') THEN email
    ELSE 'REDACTED'
  END AS email,
  country,
  product,
  total
FROM sales_raw
```

Using dynamic views you can specify permissions down to the row or field level. Consider the following example, where only users who belong to the `managers` group are able to see transaction amounts (`total` column) greater than $1,000,000.00:

```
CREATE VIEW sales_redacted AS
SELECT
  user_id,
  country,
  product,
  total
FROM sales_raw
WHERE
  CASE
    WHEN is_group_member('managers') THEN TRUE
    ELSE total <= 1000000
  END;
```

As shown in the preceding examples, you can implement column-level masking to prevent users from seeing specific column data unless they are in the correct group. Because these views are standard Spark SQL, you can do more advanced types of masking with more complex SQL expressions. The following example lets all users perform analysis on email domains, but lets members of the `auditors` group see users' full email addresses.

```
-- The regexp_extract function takes an email address such as
-- user.x.lastname@example.com and extracts 'example', allowing
-- analysts to query the domain name
CREATE VIEW sales_redacted AS
SELECT
  user_id,
  region,
  CASE
    WHEN is_group_member('auditors') THEN email
    ELSE regexp_extract(email, '^.*@(.*)$', 1)
  END
  FROM sales_raw
```

reference_note.title: Dynamic Views for Column and Row-Level Permissions in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Databricks provides two functions—`current_user()` and `is_member()`—that let you control who sees what data in views. You can use these functions inside view definitions to mask columns (hide sensitive data) or filter rows (show only allowed records) based on the user's group membership. This is done using standard SQL CASE statements, so Spark can still optimize performance.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A view that changes what data it shows depending on who is querying it. Instead of showing the same data to everyone, the view uses functions to check the current user's group membership and returns different data accordingly.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In real projects, you often need to share data with multiple teams but restrict access to sensitive columns or rows. Dynamic views let you do this without creating separate tables or views for each group.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Hiding or transforming the content of specific columns for users who don't have permission to see them. For example, showing 'REDACTED' instead of an email address, or showing only the email domain instead of the full address.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Protects sensitive data like emails, phone numbers, or salary information while still allowing other users to work with the table.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Showing or hiding entire rows based on the current user's group membership. For example, a manager might see all transactions, but a regular analyst only sees transactions under $1,000,000.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Ensures users only see data they are authorized to access, which is critical for compliance and data governance in real projects.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Users are organized into groups at the workspace level in Databricks. The `is_member()` function checks if the current user belongs to a specific group.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Groups are the mechanism Databricks uses to manage permissions at scale. Instead of setting permissions for each user individually, you assign users to groups and set permissions for groups.

important_features_or_tools.name: current_user()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Returns the name of the user currently running the query.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to log or identify which user is accessing data, or when you want to show user-specific data.

important_features_or_tools.name: is_member()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Checks if the current user is a member of a specific Databricks group at the workspace level. Returns true if the user is in the group, false otherwise.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to grant permissions based on group membership. Use this inside CASE statements in views to conditionally show or hide data.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of the Databricks group to check membership against

important_features_or_tools.name: Dynamic View with CASE Statement
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A view that uses CASE WHEN is_member() THEN ... ELSE ... END to conditionally return different data based on the user's group membership.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you need to implement column-level masking or row-level filtering in a single view that all users can query.

important_features_or_tools.name: Hive Metastore
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: The metadata store where Databricks manages table and view definitions. Dynamic views with permission logic are managed by the Hive metastore.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: You don't directly interact with the Hive metastore, but you should know that your permission views are stored there and work with standard Spark SQL.

important_features_or_tools.name: regexp_extract()
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Spark SQL function that extracts part of a string using a regular expression. In the example, it extracts the email domain from a full email address.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want to mask sensitive data by showing only a part of it. For example, showing the email domain but hiding the username part.

important_parameters.meaning: The input string to extract from
The regular expression pattern to match
Which captured group from the regex to return (1-indexed)

practical_workflow.action: Identify which groups exist in your Databricks workspace and which users belong to each group.
practical_workflow.reason: You need to know the exact group names to use in `is_member()` calls, and understand who should have access to what data.

practical_workflow.action: Identify which columns or rows need to be restricted and which groups should have access to them.
practical_workflow.reason: This determines what permission logic you need to write in your view definition.

practical_workflow.action: Create a view using CREATE VIEW that wraps the original table with CASE WHEN is_member() logic.
practical_workflow.reason: The view becomes the single source of truth for data access. Users query the view instead of the raw table.

practical_workflow.action: For column-level masking: use CASE WHEN is_member() THEN column_name ELSE 'REDACTED' (or transformed value) END AS column_name.
practical_workflow.reason: This shows the real column value to authorized users and a masked value to everyone else.

practical_workflow.action: For row-level filtering: add a WHERE clause with CASE WHEN is_member() THEN TRUE ELSE condition END.
practical_workflow.reason: This filters which rows are visible based on group membership.

practical_workflow.action: Test the view by querying it as different users (or users in different groups) to verify the permissions work correctly.
practical_workflow.reason: Ensures that the permission logic is correct and users only see what they should.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking you need to create separate views for each group.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: A single dynamic view can serve all groups. The CASE statement inside the view automatically returns different data based on who is querying it.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting to alias masked columns (e.g., AS email) when using CASE statements.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Always alias the CASE expression to the original column name. This prevents the permission logic from appearing in the column name and keeps the view interface clean.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming dynamic views have poor performance because they include conditional logic.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Spark optimizes CASE statements at analysis time, replacing them with the literal value or column reference that applies to the current user. Performance is not degraded.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using `is_group_member()` instead of `is_member()`.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The correct function name is `is_member()`. It checks if the current user is a member of a workspace-level group.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking the view protects data at the table level.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The view only protects data when users query the view. If users have direct access to the underlying table, they can bypass the view's permissions. Restrict table access and direct users to the view.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, create a view for each sensitive table. For example, if you have a sales_raw table with sensitive data, create sales_redacted as the public view and restrict direct access to sales_raw.
Use group names that match your organization's structure (e.g., 'auditors', 'managers', 'finance_team'). Make sure these groups are created in your Databricks workspace before writing the views.
Combine multiple permission checks in a single view. For example, you can mask the email column AND filter rows based on different group memberships in the same view.
For complex masking (like showing only email domains), use Spark SQL functions like regexp_extract() inside the CASE statement. This keeps the logic in SQL and maintains performance.
Document which groups have access to which columns and rows in your views. This helps other team members understand the permission model and prevents accidental data exposure.
Test views with users from different groups before deploying to production. Verify that each group sees exactly what they should and nothing more.

source_content:
This article describes how to enable table access control for the built-in Hive metastore on a cluster.

For information about how to set privileges on Hive metastore securable objects once table access control has been enabled on a cluster, see Hive metastore privileges and securable objects (legacy).

Hive metastore table access control is a legacy data governance model. Databricks recommends that you use Unity Catalog instead for its simplicity and account-centered governance model. You can upgrade the tables managed by the Hive metastore to the Unity Catalog metastore.

Table access control is available in two versions:

- SQL-only table access control, which restricts users to SQL commands.
- Python and SQL table access control, which allows users to run SQL, Python, and PySpark commands.

Table access control is not supported with Machine Learning Runtime.

Even if table access control is enabled for a cluster, Databricks workspace administrators have access to file-level data.

This version of table access control restricts users to SQL commands only.

To enable SQL-only table access control on a cluster and restrict that cluster to use only SQL commands, set the following flag in the cluster's Spark conf:

```
spark.databricks.acl.sqlOnly true
```
Access to SQL-only table access control is not affected by the Enable Table Access Control setting in the admin settings page. That setting controls only the workspace-wide enablement of Python and SQL table access control.

This version of table access control lets users run Python commands that use the DataFrame API as well as SQL. When it is enabled on a cluster, users on that cluster:

- Can access Spark only using the Spark SQL API or DataFrame API. In both cases, access to tables and views is restricted by administrators according to the Databricks Privileges you can grant on Hive metastore objects.
- Must run their commands on cluster nodes as a low-privilege user forbidden from accessing sensitive parts of the filesystem or creating network connections to ports other than 80 and 443.
- Only built-in Spark functions can create network connections on ports other than 80 and 443.
- Only workspace admin users or users with ANY FILE privilege can read data from external databases through the PySpark JDBC connector.
- If you want Python processes to be able to access additional outbound ports, you can set the Spark config `spark.databricks.pyspark.iptable.outbound.whitelisted.ports`to the ports you want to allow access. The supported format of the configuration value is`[port[:port][,port[:port]]...]`, for example:`21,22,9000:9999`. The port must be within the valid range, that is,`0-65535`.

Attempts to get around these restrictions will fail with an exception. These restrictions are in place so that users can never access unprivileged data through the cluster.

Before users can configure Python and SQL table access control, a Databricks workspace admin must enable table access control for the Databricks workspace and deny users access to clusters that are not enabled for table access control.

- Go to the settings page.
- Click the **Security**tab.
- Turn on the **Table Access Control**option.

To ensure that your users access only the data that you want them to, you must restrict your users to clusters with table access control enabled. In particular, you should ensure that:

- Users do not have permission to create clusters. If they create a cluster without table access control, they can access any data from that cluster.
- Users do not have CAN ATTACH TO permission for any cluster that is not enabled for table access control.

See Compute permissions for more information.

Table access control is enabled by default in clusters with Standard access mode.

To create the cluster using the REST API, see Create new cluster.

reference_note.title: Enabling Table Access Control on Hive Metastore Clusters
reference_note.summary: Table access control restricts what data users can access on a Databricks cluster. There are two versions: SQL-only (restricts to SQL commands) and Python and SQL (allows DataFrame API and SQL). You enable it by setting a Spark configuration flag on the cluster, and workspace admins must configure workspace-wide settings to enforce it. Note that Databricks recommends using Unity Catalog instead, which is the modern approach.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: A security feature that controls which tables and views users can access on a cluster. It prevents users from accessing data they shouldn't see.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In real projects, you need to ensure sensitive data is only accessible to authorized users. TAC enforces this at the cluster level.

key_concepts.concept: SQL-only vs. Python and SQL table access control
key_concepts.simple_explanation: SQL-only restricts users to SQL commands only. Python and SQL allows users to also run Python and PySpark commands with DataFrame API, but with additional security restrictions.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: You choose based on what your users need to do. If they only need SQL, use SQL-only for simpler restrictions. If they need Python, use the Python and SQL version with stricter security rules.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Table access control on Hive metastore is the older way to control data access. Unity Catalog is the newer, recommended approach.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: For new projects, you should use Unity Catalog instead. If you have existing Hive metastore tables, you can upgrade them to Unity Catalog.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Workspace admins must enable table access control at the workspace level and prevent users from accessing clusters without it.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Without admin enforcement, users can create or access clusters without access control, defeating the security purpose.

important_features_or_tools.name: spark.databricks.acl.sqlOnly
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: When set to true, enables SQL-only table access control on a cluster, restricting users to SQL commands only.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When you want the simplest form of table access control and users only need to run SQL queries.

important_parameters.meaning: Set to 'true' to enable SQL-only mode

important_features_or_tools.name: spark.databricks.pyspark.iptable.outbound.whitelisted.ports
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Specifies which outbound network ports Python processes can access when Python and SQL table access control is enabled. By default, only ports 80 and 443 are allowed.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When users need to connect to external databases or services on non-standard ports using PySpark JDBC connector.

important_parameters.meaning: Comma-separated list of ports or port ranges to allow

important_features_or_tools.name: Table Access Control setting (Admin Settings)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A workspace-level toggle in the Security tab that enables Python and SQL table access control for the entire workspace.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When a workspace admin wants to enforce table access control across the workspace for all clusters that support it.

important_parameters.meaning: Found in Settings > Security tab

important_features_or_tools.name: Standard access mode
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A cluster access mode that has table access control enabled by default.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When creating clusters where you want table access control to be automatically active.

important_features_or_tools.name: Compute permissions
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: Permissions that control whether users can create clusters or attach to existing clusters.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: When admins need to prevent users from creating or accessing clusters without table access control.

important_parameters.meaning: Permission that allows a user to attach to a cluster. Should be denied for clusters without table access control.

practical_workflow.action: As a workspace admin, go to Settings > Security tab and turn on the Table Access Control option
practical_workflow.reason: This enables table access control at the workspace level, allowing clusters to enforce it.

practical_workflow.action: Decide which version you need: SQL-only or Python and SQL
practical_workflow.reason: This determines what commands your users can run and what security restrictions apply.

practical_workflow.action: For SQL-only: Set spark.databricks.acl.sqlOnly true in the cluster's Spark conf
practical_workflow.reason: This enables SQL-only table access control on that specific cluster.

practical_workflow.action: For Python and SQL: Use Standard access mode when creating the cluster (table access control is enabled by default)
practical_workflow.reason: Standard access mode automatically enables Python and SQL table access control.

practical_workflow.action: Restrict user permissions: prevent users from creating clusters and deny CAN ATTACH TO permission for clusters without table access control
practical_workflow.reason: This ensures users can only access clusters where table access control is enforced.

practical_workflow.action: If users need access to non-standard ports, set spark.databricks.pyspark.iptable.outbound.whitelisted.ports in the cluster Spark conf
practical_workflow.reason: By default, only ports 80 and 443 are allowed for security. You must explicitly allow other ports if needed.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that enabling Table Access Control in admin settings automatically secures all clusters
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: The admin setting only enables the feature workspace-wide. You must still configure individual clusters (SQL-only flag or Standard access mode) and restrict user permissions to prevent them from accessing unsecured clusters.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming workspace admins cannot access data protected by table access control
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Workspace admins have file-level data access regardless of table access control settings. Table access control restricts regular users, not admins.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Using table access control with Machine Learning Runtime
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Table access control is not supported with Machine Learning Runtime. You must use a different cluster type.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking SQL-only and Python and SQL table access control are the same
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: SQL-only restricts users to SQL commands only. Python and SQL allows DataFrame API and Python but with stricter security rules (low-privilege user, limited filesystem access, limited network ports).

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Allowing users to create clusters without table access control
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Users who can create clusters can bypass table access control by creating a cluster without it. Always prevent users from creating clusters or restrict them to pre-configured clusters with table access control enabled.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, start by deciding: do your users need Python/PySpark or just SQL? This determines which table access control version to use.
Always have a workspace admin configure the workspace-level Table Access Control setting first, then configure individual clusters.
For SQL-only projects (e.g., analytics teams using SQL queries), use SQL-only table access control for simplicity.
For data science projects requiring Python, use Python and SQL table access control, but be aware of the security restrictions (low-privilege user, limited network access).
Consider upgrading to Unity Catalog instead of using Hive metastore table access control, as it is the modern recommended approach.
Always restrict user permissions to prevent cluster creation and unauthorized cluster access. This is critical for table access control to work.
If users need to connect to external databases on non-standard ports, you must explicitly configure spark.databricks.pyspark.iptable.outbound.whitelisted.ports.
Remember that workspace admins can always access file-level data, so table access control is for regular users only.

source_content:
In Unity Catalog, all catalogs are accessible by default from any workspace attached to the same metastore. Workspace-catalog binding lets you override this default to restrict a catalog to one or more specific workspaces. Access from an unbound workspace is denied, even for users with explicit privilege grants on the catalog.

Organizational and compliance requirements often specify that certain data must remain accessible only in designated environments. You may also need to:

- Isolate production data from development or test environments.
- Prevent certain data domains from being joined together.
- Ensure that sensitive data can only be processed in specific workspaces.

In Databricks, the workspace is the primary data processing environment, and the catalog is the primary data domain. Workspace-catalog binding connects these two concepts, letting catalog owners and users with the `MANAGE` privilege define which workspaces can access which catalogs.

When you bind a catalog to specific workspaces, only the workspaces you assign can access the catalog. Any workspace not in the assigned list receives an error when users try to access the catalog, overriding any individual privilege grants those users hold.

In this diagram, `prod_catalog` is bound to two production workspaces. Even if a user holds a `SELECT` grant on a table in `prod_catalog`, they cannot access that table from the Dev workspace.

When binding a catalog to a workspace, you can optionally restrict that workspace to read-only access. All write operations from that workspace to the catalog are blocked.

The exception to the default open behavior is the default workspace catalog created automatically for all new workspaces. This workspace catalog is bound only to its own workspace by default. If you unbind this catalog or extend access to other workspaces, you must grant any required permissions manually, because the workspace admins group is workspace-local and cannot be used across workspaces.

Workspace-catalog bindings are enforced consistently across the platform:

- Information schema queries return only the catalogs accessible in the current workspace.
- Data lineage and Catalog Explorer show only catalogs that are assigned to the current workspace.

Workspace binding applies beyond catalogs. You can also bind:

- **External locations**: restrict which workspaces can access specific cloud storage paths. See Assign an external location to specific workspaces.
- **Storage credentials**: restrict which workspaces can use specific cloud credentials. See Assign a storage credential to specific workspaces.

- **Service credentials**: restrict which workspaces can use specific cloud service credentials. See (Optional) Assign a service credential to specific workspaces.

When a catalog is bound to specific workspaces, users in unbound workspaces cannot access it, even if they have explicit permissions.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming that individual user permissions (like SELECT grants) will allow access from any workspace
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Workspace-catalog binding is enforced at the workspace level and overrides individual permissions. A user must be in a workspace that is bound to the catalog, regardless of their individual privileges.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that unbinding a workspace catalog automatically grants permissions to users in other workspaces
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: When you unbind or extend access to a workspace catalog, you must manually grant permissions because workspace admin groups are workspace-local and cannot be used across workspaces.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting that binding applies to Information schema queries, Catalog Explorer, and data lineage
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Workspace-catalog bindings are enforced consistently across the platform. Users will only see catalogs they have access to in all these tools.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking workspace-catalog binding is the only way to restrict workspace access to data
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You can also bind external locations, storage credentials, and service credentials to specific workspaces for more granular control.

project_usage_notes: In a real project, use workspace-catalog binding to isolate production catalogs from development workspaces. For example, bind prod_catalog only to production workspaces and enable read-only access for any development workspaces that need to analyze production data.

When setting up a multi-team data platform, bind different catalogs to different teams' workspaces to prevent accidental data joins between sensitive domains (e.g., keep customer data separate from financial data).

For compliance-heavy projects, workspace-catalog binding provides audit-friendly data isolation. Access is denied at the workspace level, so you don't have to rely solely on row-level or column-level security.

When creating a new workspace, remember that its default workspace catalog is bound only to that workspace. If you need to share it with other workspaces, you must explicitly unbind it and manually grant permissions.
Use read-only binding for development and test workspaces that need to access production catalogs for analysis or testing without risking accidental data modifications.
Workspace-catalog binding works alongside external location and storage credential binding. Use all three together for comprehensive workspace-level access control over both data and cloud resources.

source_content:
To assign a catalog to specific workspaces, you can use Catalog Explorer or the Databricks CLI.

**Permissions required**: Metastore admin, catalog owner, or `MANAGE` and `USE CATALOG` on the catalog.

Regardless of whether a catalog is assigned to the current workspace, metastore admins can see all catalogs in a metastore, and catalog owners can see all catalogs they own in a metastore. Catalogs that aren't assigned to the workspace appear grayed out, and no child objects are visible or queryable.

- Catalog Explorer
- CLI

-
Log in to a workspace that is linked to the metastore.
-
Click **Catalog**.
-
In the **Catalog**pane, on the left, click the catalog name.The main Catalog Explorer pane defaults to the **Catalogs**list. You can also select the catalog there.
-
On the **Workspaces**tab, clear the**All workspaces have access**checkbox.If your catalog is already bound to one or more workspaces, this checkbox is already cleared.
-
Click **Assign to workspaces**and enter or find the workspaces you want to assign.
-
(Optional) Limit workspace access to read-only. On the **Manage Access Level**menu, select**Change access to read-only**.You can reverse this selection at any time by editing the catalog and selecting **Change access to read & write**.

To revoke access, go to the **Workspaces** tab, select the workspace, and click **Revoke**.

There are two Databricks CLI command groups and two steps required to assign a catalog to a workspace.

In the following examples, replace `<profile-name>` with the name of your Databricks authentication configuration profile. It should include the value of a personal access token, in addition to the workspace instance name and workspace ID of the workspace where you generated the personal access token. See Personal access token authentication (legacy).

-
Use the `catalogs`command group's`update`command to set the catalog's`isolation mode`to`ISOLATED`:Bash`databricks catalogs update <my-catalog> \`
 --isolation-mode ISOLATED \
 --profile <profile-name>The default `isolation-mode`is`OPEN`to all workspaces attached to the metastore.
-
Use the `workspace-bindings`command group's`update-bindings`command to assign the workspaces to the catalog:Bash`databricks workspace-bindings update-bindings catalog <my-catalog> \`
 --json '{
 "add": [{"workspace_id": <workspace-id>, "binding_type": <binding-type>}...],
 "remove": [{"workspace_id": <workspace-id>, "binding_type": "<binding-type>}...]
 }' --profile <profile-name>Use the `"add"`and`"remove"`properties to add or remove workspace bindings. The`<binding-type>`can be either`"BINDING_TYPE_READ_WRITE"`(default) or`"BINDING_TYPE_READ_ONLY"`.

To list all workspace assignments for a catalog, use the `workspace-bindings` command group's `get-bindings` command:

```
databricks workspace-bindings get-bindings catalog <my-catalog> \
--profile <profile-name>
```

Instructions for revoking workspace access to a catalog using Catalog Explorer or the `workspace-bindings` CLI command group are included in Bind a catalog to one or more workspaces.

If your workspace was enabled for Unity Catalog automatically and you have a default workspace catalog, workspace admins own that catalog and have all permissions on that catalog **in the workspace only**. If you unbind that catalog or bind it to other catalogs, you must grant any required permissions manually to the members of the workspace admins group as individual users or using account-level groups, because the workspace admins group is a workspace-local group. For more information about account groups vs workspace-local groups, see Group sources.

reference_note.title: Assigning Catalogs to Workspaces in Databricks
reference_note.summary: Catalogs in Databricks can be assigned to specific workspaces using Catalog Explorer or the CLI. By default, catalogs are open to all workspaces in a metastore, but you can restrict access by setting isolation mode to ISOLATED and then binding specific workspaces. You can also set access levels to read-only if needed. Only metastore admins, catalog owners, or users with MANAGE and USE CATALOG permissions can perform these tasks.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: Controls whether a catalog is available to all workspaces (OPEN mode, the default) or restricted to specific workspaces (ISOLATED mode). In OPEN mode, all workspaces attached to the metastore can access the catalog. In ISOLATED mode, only workspaces you explicitly assign can access it.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: When working on a real project, you may want to restrict data access to specific teams or workspaces. Setting isolation mode to ISOLATED is the first step to controlling which workspaces can see and use a catalog.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: The assignment of a catalog to one or more specific workspaces. Once a catalog is in ISOLATED mode, you create bindings to specify which workspaces can access it and what level of access they have (read-only or read-write).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Workspace bindings let you control data governance and security by ensuring only the right teams can access specific catalogs in your Databricks environment.

key_concepts.simple_explanation: When assigning a catalog to a workspace, you can choose whether that workspace has read-only access (can query data but not modify it) or read-write access (can query and modify data).
key_concepts.why_it_matters: In a real project, you may want some teams to only view data while others can modify it. This setting enforces that control at the catalog level.

key_concepts.concept: Metastore Admin and Catalog Owner Permissions
key_concepts.simple_explanation: Metastore admins can see and manage all catalogs in a metastore. Catalog owners can see and manage only the catalogs they own. Both can assign catalogs to workspaces. Regular users cannot perform these tasks.
key_concepts.why_it_matters: Understanding who has permission to assign catalogs helps you know whether you need to request help from an admin or if you have the necessary permissions to set up your project's data access.

important_features_or_tools.name: Catalog Explorer
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A UI in the Databricks workspace where you can view catalogs, assign them to workspaces, set access levels, and revoke access. Catalogs not assigned to the current workspace appear grayed out.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this when you prefer a graphical interface to manage catalog assignments. It's the easiest method for beginners.

important_features_or_tools.name: catalogs update command
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks CLI command that updates a catalog's isolation mode. You use this to change a catalog from OPEN (default) to ISOLATED so you can restrict it to specific workspaces.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this as the first step when assigning a catalog to specific workspaces via CLI. You must run this before using workspace-bindings commands.

important_parameters.meaning: Sets whether the catalog is available to all workspaces (OPEN) or only to explicitly assigned workspaces (ISOLATED)
The name of your Databricks authentication configuration profile, which includes your personal access token and workspace details

important_features_or_tools.name: workspace-bindings update-bindings command
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks CLI command that assigns or removes workspaces from a catalog. You specify which workspaces to add or remove and what access level each should have.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this after setting isolation mode to ISOLATED. This command actually creates the bindings between the catalog and specific workspaces.

important_parameters.meaning: A list of workspaces to assign to the catalog, each with a workspace_id and binding_type
A list of workspaces to remove from the catalog, each with a workspace_id and binding_type
Controls the access level: BINDING_TYPE_READ_WRITE (default) allows reading and writing; BINDING_TYPE_READ_ONLY allows only reading
The name of your Databricks authentication configuration profile

important_features_or_tools.name: workspace-bindings get-bindings command
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A Databricks CLI command that lists all workspace assignments for a specific catalog, showing which workspaces have access and their access levels.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this to verify which workspaces are currently assigned to a catalog and what their access levels are.

important_parameters.meaning: The name of your Databricks authentication configuration profile

important_features_or_tools.name: Workspaces Tab (in Catalog Explorer)
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A section in Catalog Explorer where you can see which workspaces have access to a catalog, manage access levels, and revoke access. The 'All workspaces have access' checkbox shows whether the catalog is in OPEN or ISOLATED mode.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this in Catalog Explorer to view and modify workspace assignments for a catalog.

important_parameters.meaning: When checked, the catalog is in OPEN mode (available to all workspaces). When unchecked, the catalog is in ISOLATED mode (available only to assigned workspaces).

important_features_or_tools.name: Manage Access Level menu
important_features_or_tools.what_it_does: A menu in Catalog Explorer that lets you change a workspace's access to a catalog between read-only and read-write.
important_features_or_tools.when_to_use_it: Use this when you want to restrict a workspace to read-only access after assigning a catalog to it.

important_parameters.meaning: Restricts the workspace to querying data only; modifications are not allowed
Allows the workspace to both query and modify data in the catalog

practical_workflow.action: Check your permissions: Verify you are a metastore admin, catalog owner, or have MANAGE and USE CATALOG permissions on the catalog you want to assign.
practical_workflow.reason: Only users with these permissions can assign catalogs to workspaces. If you don't have them, you'll need to ask an admin for help.

practical_workflow.action: Choose your method: Decide whether to use Catalog Explorer (UI) or the Databricks CLI (command line).
practical_workflow.reason: Catalog Explorer is easier for beginners; CLI is faster for automation and scripting.

practical_workflow.action: If using Catalog Explorer: Log in to a workspace linked to the metastore, click Catalog, select your catalog name, go to the Workspaces tab, and uncheck 'All workspaces have access' if it's checked.
practical_workflow.reason: This puts the catalog into ISOLATED mode so you can restrict it to specific workspaces.

practical_workflow.action: If using CLI: Run 'databricks catalogs update <my-catalog> --isolation-mode ISOLATED --profile <profile-name>' to set the catalog to ISOLATED mode.
practical_workflow.reason: This is the first CLI step required before you can bind specific workspaces to the catalog.

practical_workflow.action: If using Catalog Explorer: Click 'Assign to workspaces' and enter or find the workspaces you want to assign. Optionally, set access to read-only using the 'Manage Access Level' menu.
practical_workflow.reason: This creates the actual bindings between the catalog and the workspaces you select.

practical_workflow.action: If using CLI: Run 'databricks workspace-bindings update-bindings catalog <my-catalog> --json {...}' with your workspace IDs and binding types (BINDING_TYPE_READ_WRITE or BINDING_TYPE_READ_ONLY).
practical_workflow.reason: This creates the bindings and sets the access level for each workspace.

practical_workflow.action: Verify your assignments: Use Catalog Explorer or run 'databricks workspace-bindings get-bindings catalog <my-catalog> --profile <profile-name>' to confirm the bindings are correct.
practical_workflow.reason: This ensures your catalog is assigned to the right workspaces with the correct access levels before your team starts using it.

practical_workflow.action: If you need to revoke access later: In Catalog Explorer, go to the Workspaces tab, select the workspace, and click Revoke. Or use the CLI 'remove' property in the workspace-bindings update-bindings command.
practical_workflow.reason: You may need to remove workspace access if a team no longer needs the catalog or if access was granted by mistake.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Thinking that a catalog is automatically restricted to a workspace when you create it.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: By default, catalogs are in OPEN mode and available to all workspaces in the metastore. You must explicitly set isolation mode to ISOLATED and then bind specific workspaces to restrict access.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Trying to assign a catalog to a workspace without first setting isolation mode to ISOLATED.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: You must always set isolation mode to ISOLATED first (either via Catalog Explorer by unchecking 'All workspaces have access' or via CLI with the catalogs update command). Only then can you assign specific workspaces.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Assuming that grayed-out catalogs in Catalog Explorer are unavailable or broken.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: Catalogs appear grayed out when they are not assigned to the current workspace. This is normal. Metastore admins and catalog owners can still see and manage them; other users simply cannot access them in that workspace.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Forgetting that workspace admins group permissions are workspace-local and don't transfer when a catalog is unbound or rebound.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: If you unbind a default workspace catalog or bind it to other workspaces, the workspace admins group loses its automatic permissions. You must manually grant permissions to individual users or account-level groups.

common_mistakes_or_confusions.mistake: Confusing BINDING_TYPE_READ_WRITE and BINDING_TYPE_READ_ONLY in CLI commands.
common_mistakes_or_confusions.correction: BINDING_TYPE_READ_WRITE (the default) allows both reading and writing. BINDING_TYPE_READ_ONLY allows only reading. Choose based on whether the workspace needs to modify data in the catalog.

project_usage_notes: When starting a real Databricks project, decide early which catalogs should be shared across all workspaces (leave in OPEN mode) and which should be restricted to specific teams (set to ISOLATED mode and bind only the needed workspaces). This prevents accidental data access and keeps your data governance clean.

If your project has multiple teams working on different datasets, use workspace bindings to ensure each team's workspace can only access the catalogs they need. Use read-only access for teams that should only view data, not modify it.

If you're automating catalog setup for multiple workspaces, use the CLI commands (catalogs update and workspace-bindings update-bindings) in a script. This is faster and more reliable than using Catalog Explorer for each workspace.

Always verify your workspace bindings after setting them up using get-bindings or by checking Catalog Explorer. This ensures your team can actually access the catalogs they need before they start their work.

If you have a default workspace catalog created automatically when Unity Catalog was enabled, be aware that workspace admins lose automatic permissions if you unbind or rebind it. Plan to grant permissions manually to avoid access issues.
